sections.title: Module 9 — Directing Access Testing and Facing the Auditor

blocks.text: Module 9 — Directing Access Testing and Facing the Auditor

Six sessions, about nine hours. This module is a lead companion: read it with Session 17 and the seven access sessions of Method Manual Part 3A, which teach how each test is done. Here you learn what the lead directs, checks and decides, using Corvane's real test record. The module quiz and case review CR-S9 are practice only.

rows: The seven access controls and their tests
Reading an access workpaper as a lead
From exception to deficiency: severity and grouping
Privileged access and reliance on automated controls
Remediation, retest and the auditor conversation

sections.title: Session 9.1 — The Seven Access Controls and Their Tests

blocks.text: Session 9.1 — The Seven Access Controls and Their Tests

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Name the seven Corvane access controls. Read their test results for the baseline period. Say which the security workstream owns.

blocks.text: Every access control was tested twice: a test of design (TOD, one walkthrough) and a test of operating effectiveness (TOE, a sample from the population) for the period 1 January to 31 May 2026. S. Boateng tested and T. Adeyemi reviewed all fourteen access tests.

rows: Privileged, generic and default IDs controlled
Password and logon parameters set to policy
Database and OS privileged access restricted

blocks.text: All seven designs were effective; six of seven failed in operation. That pattern, good design and weak operation, says the controls were written well and run carelessly. It points the remediation at people, workload and monitoring, not at redesign.

rows: PM LENS A plan that is right on paper and missed in delivery needs execution discipline, not a new plan. Read test results the same way.
TRY IT 9.1 Which of the seven controls does the security workstream own outright, which does it share, and which belongs to Basis? Use W07.

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. What is the difference between TOD and TOE?
2. What did six effective designs and six failed operations tell the lead?
3. Which access control passed operating effectiveness?

sections.title: Session 9.2 — Directing the Access Test Plan

blocks.text: Session 9.2 — Directing the Access Test Plan

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Set the order and rules of access testing. Insist on population and IPE before sampling. Check independence and timing.
No point sampling a control that cannot work
TODs 4 to 19 May; TOEs 16 to 30 June
Population before sample; IPE must pass
A sample from an incomplete list proves nothing
Every access TOE population has IPE Pass (W10)
S. Boateng tests; T. Adeyemi reviews
ITAC testing relies on ITGC results
Access TOEs end 30 June; ITAC TOEs start 14 July
25 for frequent controls; 2 or 3 for monthly or quarterly

IN THE CORVANE CASE The populations came from the system: a user and assignment listing for provisioning (EV-037), the HR leavers report for leavers (EV-039), and the EAM session log for firefighter sessions (EV-041). Each passed its completeness check before a sample was drawn (W09 IPE log). The security workstream supplied several of these populations, so its own data quality decided whether the tests could start.
PM LENS This is entry criteria for a test phase. You would not start user acceptance testing on an unfinished build; do not start sampling on an unproven population.
TRY IT 9.2 The firefighter log report for March is missing two days because of a log sync failure. What do you tell the tester, and what do you ask the GRC administrator? (Compare INC-07.)

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. Why must IPE pass before sampling?
2. Why are general controls tested before automated ones?
3. What decides sample size?

sections.title: Session 9.3 — Reading an Access Workpaper as a Lead

blocks.text: Session 9.3 — Reading an Access Workpaper as a Lead

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Know what a lead reads in an access workpaper. Challenge an exception that is explained away. Use the leavers and firefighter workpapers in W11.

blocks.text: The lead does not re-perform the test. The lead reads the workpaper for five things: the population source and its completeness, the sample selection, the test attributes, each exception and how it was evaluated, and whether the conclusion follows. The common weakness is an exception explained away ("the user did not log on after leaving, so no harm") without evidence or against the control's criteria.

rows: Does it agree to the system on the test date, with IPE Pass?
Was it drawn properly and is it the right size?
Do they test what the control promises?
Is each exception counted, or explained away?
Does the result follow from the exceptions?

IN THE CORVANE CASE The leavers workpaper (C-ITGC-AC-002) found six of 25 leavers locked after more than two business days, 6 to 14 days late. The cause, a weekly HR report, is recorded in DEF-010. The firefighter workpaper (C-ITGC-AC-004) found late reviews and two reviews that did not question unusual activity, including a vendor bank change (DEF-005). Neither exception was explained away: both became deficiencies.
PM LENS A workpaper is a test report. You would reject a test report that marks a failed case "passed with comment".
TRY IT 9.3 A tester writes: "Leaver locked 9 days late, but no logon after termination, so not an exception." Write the lead's review note.

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. Name the five things a lead reads.
2. What is "explaining away" an exception?
3. What caused the leavers exceptions?

sections.title: Session 9.4 — From Exception to Deficiency: Severity and Grouping

blocks.text: Session 9.4 — From Exception to Deficiency: Severity and Grouping

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES State the three severity levels. Explain why deficiencies are grouped by cause. Read the access groups in W13.
A control does not prevent or detect misstatement on time
Less severe than a material weakness but important enough to merit the audit committee's attention
A reasonable possibility that a material misstatement will not be prevented or detected on time

blocks.text: Deficiencies that share a cause are grouped and evaluated together, because one cause behind several failures can be more serious than any one alone. The group's severity can be higher than each member's.

rows: IN THE CORVANE CASE W13 groups Corvane's access deficiencies by cause. GR-A, privileged access governance (DEF-001, DEF-002, DEF-005, DEF-026), was rated a significant deficiency: emergency access granted informally and direct assignments outside GRC let Basis and support users bypass access controls. GR-C, access hygiene (DEF-010, DEF-011), stayed a control deficiency because the effective quarterly access review compensates. GR-F (DEF-004, HANA SYSTEM user) is a single deficiency, still open.
PM LENS Grouping by cause is root-cause analysis across a defect log. Ten defects with one cause are one big problem, not ten small ones.
TRY IT 9.4 Explain to the CFO in four sentences why GR-A was a significant deficiency when DEF-002, DEF-005 and DEF-026 were each only control deficiencies.

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. Name the three severity levels.
2. Why group by cause?
3. Why did GR-C stay a control deficiency?

sections.title: Session 9.5 — Privileged Access and Reliance on Automated Controls

blocks.text: Session 9.5 — Privileged Access and Reliance on Automated Controls

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Explain why access deficiencies threaten automated controls. Describe compensating procedures. Read the Corvane reliance decision.

blocks.text: An automated control (ITAC) such as the three-way match can be relied on only if nobody could change it or bypass it. Privileged access lets people change configuration and data directly. So an access deficiency calls into question every automated control that depends on it. The auditor then needs either a working general control or compensating evidence that no harmful change happened.

rows: IN THE CORVANE CASE DEF-001 (dialog users with SAP_ALL and generic IDs) listed four dependent automated controls: C-ITAC-001 (three-way match), C-ITAC-003 (posting periods), C-ITAC-008 (inventory valuation) and C-ITAC-009 (JV equity configuration). The compensating procedures, full-period table change logs and usage analysis of the SAP_ALL holders, were tested effective. On that basis C-ITAC-001 was relied on despite the general control exceptions (Method Manual Part 3B, Session 33).
PM LENS Reliance is a dependency in the plan. If a predecessor task failed, you either redo it or prove its output was still sound before the successor uses it.
TRY IT 9.5 Why does table logging matter to the compensating procedure for DEF-001, and which S02 finding could weaken that procedure in future?

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. Why does privileged access threaten automated controls?
2. Name the two compensating procedures for DEF-001.
3. What are the two ways to support reliance after an ITGC exception?

sections.title: Session 9.6 — Remediation, Retest and the Auditor Conversation

blocks.text: Session 9.6 — Remediation, Retest and the Auditor Conversation

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Plan remediation and retest windows. Read the retest results. Hold the auditor conversation well.

blocks.text: A deficiency closes only after a retest over a new operating period shows the fixed control working. The lead plans the fix early enough to leave that period before year end. In the conversation with the auditor the lead speaks findings before they are written, states cause and fix plainly, and never argues a result the evidence supports.

rows: IN THE CORVANE CASE By 30 September every access deficiency except DEF-004 was closed after a retest, and GR-A, the significant deficiency, was closed. The security workstream's metrics in S06 show the same story month by month: SAP_ALL holders to zero, firefighter reviews on time, leavers locked on time.

sections.title: 9.6.1 What to say and not say to the auditor

blocks.text: 9.6.1 What to say and not say to the auditor

rows: "We found it, here is the cause, here is the fix and the retest date."
"The design is sound; operation slipped because the HR report was weekly."
"Nobody was harmed, so it is not an exception."
"Here is the evidence of the compensating procedure."
"We will have it fixed by year end" without a retest window
PM LENS Treat the auditor as a key stakeholder with veto power: no surprises, facts first, commitments you can keep.
TRY IT 9.6 The auditor asks why DEF-004 is still open and whether it threatens reliance. Draft your answer.

3. Name two things never to say to the auditor.

sections.title: Module 10 — Incidents and the Production War Room

blocks.text: Module 10 — Incidents and the Production War Room

Six sessions, about eight hours. By the end you can triage an access incident, direct the diagnosis, chair a war room, communicate to senior managers and turn the lesson into a decision. The week 8 live session replays INC-09 with you in the chair.

rows: Triage in the first thirty minutes

blocks.text: Session 10.1 — Security Incidents and Priority

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Define a security incident and its categories. Set priority consistently. Read the Corvane incident log.
A business-critical process stopped for many users, or a live security breach
INC-09: 212 users could not post at quarter-end
Many users degraded, or a control or evidence system failing
INC-05: 86 users could not use SSO; INC-03: GRC under-reported BW users for six weeks
A group of users affected, or a contained security exposure
A single user with a workaround

blocks.text: Note that INC-03 affected no user directly but was still P2: a control system reporting wrong data is a security incident even when nobody notices. INC-08, one contractor still active after leaving, is P3 because the exposure was real even though small.

rows: IN THE CORVANE CASE S05 holds nine incidents from April to September 2026 in seven categories: missing authorisation, Fiori, GRC workflow, GRC connector, firefighter, identity and SSO, and role transport. Three were P1 or P2 (KPI-11 in S06).
PM LENS Priority is about business impact, not about how hard the problem is to fix. You already rank project risks that way.
TRY IT 10.1 A payroll analyst cannot run the payroll posting job two days before payday; four others can. Set the priority and justify it.

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. What makes INC-03 a P2 with no users affected?
2. What is the P1 definition?
3. Why is INC-08 more than a P4?

sections.title: Session 10.2 — Triage in the First Thirty Minutes

blocks.text: Session 10.2 — Triage in the First Thirty Minutes

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Run the first thirty minutes of an access incident. Separate an authorisation fault from an outage. Stop unsafe fixes before they start.
How many users, which process, since when? Is it security or something else?
What changed? Transports, role changes, connector or identity events in the last 24 hours
First evidence (SU53 from several users), priority set, bridge opened, first message out

blocks.text: Two rules from the first minute: no direct change in production, and no SAP_ALL or firefighter access for business users as a workaround. Emergency access is for the people fixing the problem, logged and reviewed.

rows: IN THE CORVANE CASE On 30 September the first calls came at 07:40. The P1 was declared at 07:55, with the lead chairing and Basis and GRC on the bridge. By 08:10 SU53 from five users showed F_BKPF_BUK failing for every company code, so the team treated it as an authorisation fault, not a system outage (S05 War_Room_Timeline).
PM LENS The first thirty minutes of an incident are like the first week of a recovery plan: decide what you know, what changed, and who is in charge.
TRY IT 10.2 List the three questions you would ask Viktor Hale at 08:15 on 30 September, in order.

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. What happens in the first ten minutes?
2. Name the two rules from the first minute.
3. Why take SU53 from several users?
Session 10.3 — Diagnosis Under Pressure

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Direct a diagnosis from evidence. Recognise the common incident patterns. Know when the diagnosis is complete.
Many users, same object, same day
One user; values exist in another role
Counts too low; no errors in reports
Fails before SAP; some users only
Works in GUI, empty in Fiori

blocks.text: The diagnosis is complete when the cause is proven from evidence, explains every symptom, and predicts the fix. If the fix does not work, or part of the symptom remains, the diagnosis was incomplete, as INC-09 showed at 13:20.

rows: IN THE CORVANE CASE S05 Diagnosis records 24 steps across the nine incidents, each with the tool and what it showed. Every P1 and P2 has a confirmed root cause.
PM LENS A diagnosis is a hypothesis tested by evidence. Accepting the first plausible story is how projects fix the wrong thing quickly.
TRY IT 10.3 For INC-04, write the diagnosis in three steps, naming the evidence at each step.

Session 10.4 — The War Room: INC-09

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Follow a P1 from first call to closure. Judge the decisions taken. Chair a war room.

blocks.text: Read S05 War_Room_Timeline before this session. The table below gives the decision points.

rows: Why it was right (or a lesson)
Emergency transport CEDK930440 overwrote org values in 18 derived roles
Proven by SU53, import history and role comparison
Re-import previous role versions; no direct change in production; no firefighter posting
Keeps the fix controlled and auditable
No new access risk introduced under pressure
Right authority for an emergency change
Company code 2000 still fails; master role also changed
Lesson: compare masters as well as derived roles before import
Posting window extended by four hours
All 212 users confirmed; P1 closed after about nine hours
Closure on user confirmation, not on import

IN THE CORVANE CASE The emergency transport (RCH-040) had been imported at 06:55 without a QAS test. The war room's own fix followed the full route except the QAS business test, replaced by tests with five users per company code in production after import, an accepted risk under CIO approval.
PM LENS A war room is a crisis steering committee with a 15-minute cadence: one chair, one log, decisions recorded with owners and times.

Session 10.5 — Communication

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Write incident messages for senior managers. Keep a communication rhythm. Avoid the common mistakes.
What is affected, what is known, next update time
09:05 to the CFO and Group Financial Controller: cause known, fix under way, no data loss

blocks.text: Mistakes to avoid: guessing a time to fix before the cause is known; technical detail senior managers cannot use; hiding a setback; and silence between updates.

rows: PM LENS Incident messages are status reports on a short cycle. The same rules apply: facts, impact, next step, next update.

sections.title: Session 10.6 — Root Cause, Lessons and Decisions

blocks.text: Session 10.6 — Root Cause, Lessons and Decisions

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Separate the immediate cause from the root cause. Turn a lesson into a decision. Track it in the metrics.

blocks.text: The immediate cause of INC-09 was a transport that overwrote role values. The root cause was a process that allowed an emergency role transport without a QAS test, two days before quarter-end, with no comparison of master roles. A lesson becomes real only when it changes a rule, an owner or a metric.

rows: IN THE CORVANE CASE At 17:30 on 30 September the lead agreed ADR-08: no emergency role transport without a QAS test unless the CIO approves, and a freeze on role transports in the last three days of every quarter (S06 Decisions). KPI-11 counts P1 and P2 incidents each month; the September P1 keeps it "Not met" against a target of zero.
PM LENS A lessons-learned log that changes nothing is a diary. Each lesson needs an owner, a change and a check that the change happened.

sections.title: Appendix — Model Answers to the Try It Exercises

blocks.text: Appendix — Model Answers to the Try It Exercises

rows: The IT Security Manager owns C-ITGC-AC-001 to 006 in W07, so the workstream owns those through the lead's sponsor. C-ITGC-AC-003 is performed by role owners and C-ITGC-AC-004 by firefighter controllers: shared. C-ITGC-AC-007 belongs to the Basis Lead and DBA team.

Tell the tester not to sample March until the population is complete. Ask the GRC administrator to recover the two days (from SM20 and change documents, as in INC-07), rerun the report, and redo the IPE check.
"The control requires a lock within two business days; nine days is an exception whatever happened after. Count it, record the cause, and consider the absence of logons only in evaluating severity."

The four deficiencies share one cause: emergency access and direct assignments outside GRC. Together they let Basis and support users bypass every access control, which threatened reliance on automated controls. That combined effect deserves audit committee attention. Each alone looked small; the pattern did not.

The compensating procedure relies on full-period table change logs; without table logging there is nothing to inspect. S02 LG-04 shows table logging off in CEQ 200; if a gap like that appeared in CEP, the procedure would fail.

"DEF-004 is open because the fix needs an operating period: named DBA accounts are being set up, the SYSTEM user will be locked and a quarterly review owner named; the retest runs in November, due 18 December. On reliance, the HANA audit log analysis showed no changes to financial tables in the period, and it was tested effective as the compensating control. We will share the retest result as soon as it is reviewed."

sections.title: Chapter 1 — Week Nine: Arriving in the Middle

blocks.text: Chapter 1 — Week Nine: Arriving in the Middle

I joined the Corvane project on 9 March 2026, in its ninth week. Daniel Reyes had been running it since January and had built the foundation workbooks with his team. The first access test designs were weeks away, but the evidence requests had already shown what the tests would find. Daniel's words on my first morning were simple: "The testing will find the problems. I need someone who can fix them and keep them fixed."

I did what Daniel had done in January and spent my first days listening. I asked Raymond Okafor, Priya Raman, Neil Abernathy, Viktor Hale and Lena Varga the same three questions: what worries you about access, what has already been tried, and what must I not do?

Viktor's answer explained half of what followed. During the 2025 upgrade, when the system moved from ECC to S/4HANA, his team had needed fast access to meet the go-live date. Emergency access was granted informally, a few people kept SAP_ALL, and some generic IDs stayed active. Nobody withdrew any of it. "I know what you will find," he said. "I would rather fix it than read about it."

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT Start with a plan for privileged access or with a full assessment of the role model? I chose privileged access: it was the highest risk, Viktor wanted to own it, and it would be tested first.
WHAT I LEARNED Arriving mid-project, my first job was not to redo the foundation but to find the one problem everyone already knew about and give its owner a way to fix it with dignity.

blocks.text: Discussion
1. Why did Amara give Viktor the lead on privileged access rather than her own team?
2. What would have been lost by starting with a full role assessment?

sections.title: Chapter 2 — Privileged Access: Nine Users and Four Generic IDs

blocks.text: Chapter 2 — Privileged Access: Nine Users and Four Generic IDs

Nine dialog users in CEP held SAP_ALL, and four generic IDs were active. The monthly privileged access review had not been done in February or April because its owner had left in January. I wrote the decision down on 23 March as ADR-03: remove SAP_ALL from every dialog user, retire the generic IDs, and route emergency work through named firefighter IDs with reason codes and reviewed logs.

We did not remove everything on day one. Usage analysis showed which of the nine used SAP_ALL for real tasks, and each got a task role before the profile was removed. The count went from nine in April to six in May, three in June and zero in July. The generic IDs went faster: two by May, none by June. When the testers sampled the privileged access reviews in June, the control failed for the baseline period (DEF-001), as everyone expected. By then the fix was already running.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT Remove SAP_ALL immediately and risk stopping Basis work, or stage it with usage evidence? I staged it, with a date for each user, and reported the count every month.
WHAT I LEARNED A privileged-access fix that breaks operations gets reversed within a week. A staged fix with a number on it gets finished.

blocks.text: Discussion
1. What evidence made the staged removal defensible to the auditor?
2. Why did the baseline test still fail even though the fix had started?

sections.title: Chapter 3 — The Debt from the Conversion

blocks.text: Chapter 3 — The Debt from the Conversion

In April I looked at the role catalogue for the first time: 418 single roles and 41 composites for 1,291 users. Sixty-three roles still carried the old Z_ names from ECC and were held by 214 users. A usage study over the first twelve months on S/4HANA showed that 37 percent of the transactions in assigned roles had never been used. SU25 had not been finished after the conversion, so 112 roles carried outdated authorisation defaults.

Two incidents in April taught the team how to read access problems. On 8 April fourteen finance users in company code 3000 could not post journals: a role change the day before had dropped the company-code value (INC-01). On 22 April a treasury analyst could not run the payment proposal, but nothing was missing: she held a legacy role and a new composite, and ran the program from the wrong company code (INC-02). The first needed a fix; the second needed an explanation.
On 28 April Priya Raman approved ADR-04: redesign the legacy roles into the ZC_ standard and retire them all by 31 December. Two of them still had no owner.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT Patch the legacy roles or redesign them? Redesign was slower but ended the problem; patching would have left the same roles to fail next year.
WHAT I LEARNED Migration residue does not announce itself. It shows up as unused access, odd incidents and roles nobody owns, and it has to be paid back on a plan.

blocks.text: Discussion
1. What is the risk of retiring legacy roles too fast before year-end close?
2. Why does INC-02 matter as much as INC-01 for training a team?
Chapter 4 — The Workflow That Waited

Role changes had always gone through ChaRM, with no risk simulation and often no owner sign-off. On 12 May Neil and I agreed ADR-02: from 1 June every role change would go through Business Role Management, with an ARA simulation and the role owner's approval built in. The ten earlier changes made without a simulation were documented as a transition.

Ten days later the service desk told me 23 access requests were stuck. A role owner had left, the BRF+ rule that finds the approver returned nobody, and the workflow path had no fallback. Some requests had waited 11 days (INC-04). With BRM due to start on 1 June, the timing could not have been worse: the same owner approvals were about to carry every role change too.

We went live with BRM on 1 June as planned, and Lena added a fallback agent on 2 June. From then on, a weekly check flagged any request waiting more than three days and any agent rule that returned no approver.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT Delay BRM until the workflow was fixed, or go live and fix the fallback in parallel? I kept the date: the fix was one day of work, and delaying BRM would have meant another month of unsimulated role changes.
WHAT I LEARNED Every approval route needs a vacancy plan. People leave; workflows should not notice.

blocks.text: Discussion
1. What does a fallback agent protect against beyond leavers?
2. Why document the ten earlier changes instead of redoing them?
Chapter 5 — The Silent Sync

On 15 May Lena noticed something odd: ARA showed 41 BW users when there should have been about 168. The connector to the BW system had failed every week since 6 April, when the password of its RFC user was changed. The jobs failed quietly and GRC kept reporting on old data as if nothing were wrong (INC-03). It was fixed on 18 May.

No user had been affected, but for six weeks our risk reports had been wrong. I made it a P2 and said so in the metrics pack. From then on, every Monday, Lena checked the last successful sync date of every connector.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT Report an incident nobody noticed? I did. A control system reporting wrong data is a security incident, and hiding it would have cost more trust later than reporting it cost then.
WHAT I LEARNED The most dangerous status report is green, confident and wrong. Check the age of the data before you trust the result.

blocks.text: Discussion
1. How could a simple count reconciliation have caught INC-03 earlier?
2. Why classify it as P2 when no user was affected?

sections.title: Chapter 6 — Leavers, HR and the System Nobody Owned

blocks.text: Chapter 6 — Leavers, HR and the System Nobody Owned

In April I traced how a leaver lost SAP access. The HR leavers report reached Security once a week. SuccessFactors was the HR master, and SailPoint already governed network accounts, but nobody had connected them to SAP. The leavers test in June confirmed it: six of 25 leavers locked late, some by two weeks (DEF-010).

Grace Mbeki, Tom Brennan and I had not waited for the test. We agreed two steps in April. From 4 May HR sent a daily leavers report as a stopgap. On 1 July SailPoint began sending leaver events to GRC, which locked users automatically. The share of leavers locked on time went from 76 percent in March to 96 percent by August. Then in August a contractor who had left was still active (INC-08). Contractors were created by hand in SailPoint with no end date. We added end dates for all nine.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT Fix leavers in SAP alone, or fix the flow from HR? Fixing it in SAP alone would have treated the symptom. The flow was owned by three teams; the shared metric made it one problem.
WHAT I LEARNED Access risk often lives in systems the security team does not own. Shared metrics turn three owners into one.

blocks.text: Discussion
1. Why did the quarterly access review count as a compensating control for DEF-010?
2. What is the next weakness after contractors?

sections.title: Chapter 7 — The Rule Set Nobody Trusted

blocks.text: Chapter 7 — The Rule Set Nobody Trusted

By June the role owners had stopped reading ARA reports. In the Q2 run, 196 of 889 reported conflicts were false: 22 percent. The worst rule was the joint venture rule (SOD-014): 15 of its 26 conflicts were not real, because the rule set had no organisational rules for company code 2000, the joint venture operations code.

On 23 June we agreed ADR-05: build organisational rules for company code 2000 and review the ten noisiest rules, through BRM, with Internal Audit told in advance. The false-positive share fell from 26 percent in March to 16 percent in September. The target is 10.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT Mitigate the noisy conflicts to make the numbers look better, or fix the rule set? Mitigating false conflicts would have added controls for risks that did not exist.
WHAT I LEARNED A detector that cries wolf trains people to ignore wolves. Fix the detector before asking people to trust it.

blocks.text: Discussion
1. Why tell Internal Audit before changing the rule set?
2. What is the difference between a false positive and an accepted risk?

sections.title: Chapter 8 — Single Sign-On and the Cloud We Did Not Own

blocks.text: Chapter 8 — Single Sign-On and the Cloud We Did Not Own

On 15 June Fiori single sign-on went live through SAP IAS, which trusts Microsoft Entra ID. On the first day 86 users could not sign in: their email addresses arrived in mixed case and the Fiori mapping expected lower case (INC-05). It was fixed the same day. By September 93 percent of Fiori logons used SSO.

The cloud brought quieter problems. In August we found two contractor administrators on the BTP subaccount, added directly in the cockpit, outside the provisioning service; one had no multi-factor authentication. On 25 August ADR-07 required every cloud administrator to come through IPS and SailPoint. Ariba was another gap: suppliers created there flowed into CEP, where they could be paid, and our rule set could not see the Ariba half. We proposed Ariba for the next year's controls scope.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT Bring the cloud applications into GRC now, or wait for the IAG assessment in FY2027 (ADR-01)? We waited, but covered the gaps with manual comparisons in the meantime.
WHAT I LEARNED The cloud does not remove access risk; it moves it to administrators and integrations that nobody reviews by habit.

blocks.text: Discussion
1. Why does SSO not close a finding about SAP password parameters?
2. How would you check the Ariba-to-CEP conflict before Ariba is in GRC?
Chapter 9 — The Review That Passed

The Q1 access review had shown reviewers nothing but role names, and 81 percent finished on time. For Q2 we gave every line a role description, twelve months of usage and an SoD flag. 47 reviewers covered 1,291 users and 6,455 lines; 94 percent finished on time and 39 lines were removed, all within six business days.

Then I looked at review times. Three line managers had approved every line, hundreds each, in under ten minutes. The control had passed its test. It was still not a review. I spoke to each of them and their directors, and asked for a re-review with someone from my team beside them. For Q3, any reviewer approving more than a hundred lines in under thirty minutes gets a second-level review before the campaign closes.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT Accept a passed control, or act on a quality signal no auditor had raised? I acted, quietly and directly, with the people involved.
WHAT I LEARNED Completion is not quality. The lead's job is to see the difference before the auditor does.

blocks.text: Discussion
1. Why was the rubber-stamping not a deficiency?
2. What would you do if one director refused the re-review?
Chapter 10 — Retest Season

From 17 August to 18 September the controls team retested the access controls that had failed. All five came back effective: provisioning, leavers, firefighter reviews, privileged IDs and password parameters. With them, the significant deficiency in privileged access governance (GR-A) was closed. Only the database deficiency stayed open: named DBA accounts take longer to build, and its retest is planned for November.

I sent the steering committee one page: what failed in June, what we changed, what the retest showed, and what stays open with a date. Daniel told me it was the first access update that Sofia Lindqvist, the external audit partner, had read to the end.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT Push for the database retest in September to close everything, or wait for a real operating period? We waited. A rushed retest would have been a weak one.
WHAT I LEARNED A retest is only as good as the operating period behind it. Plan fixes early enough to leave the period.

blocks.text: Discussion
1. Why did the GR-A closure matter more than any single closure?
2. What would you say to Sofia about the open database deficiency?
Chapter 11 — 30 September

At 06:55 on the last day of the quarter an emergency transport was imported into production. It was meant to correct a small issue in finance roles. It had not been tested in QAS. It replaced the company-code values in 18 derived finance roles. By 07:40 the service desk phones were ringing: 212 finance users could not post journals.

I declared a P1 at 07:55 and chaired the bridge. SU53 from five users pointed to authorisation, not an outage. By 08:40 we had the transport and the role comparison. At 08:50 I said no to fixing roles directly in production and no to firefighter posting for the business. We rebuilt the previous role versions, had a second person check them, ran an ARA simulation, and the CIO approved the change at 11:15. Three company codes worked by 12:30. Company code 2000 still failed: one master role had also been changed. We fixed and re-derived it, and by 16:45 every user was confirmed working. Priya Raman extended the posting window by four hours.
At 17:30 we agreed ADR-08: no emergency role transport without a QAS test unless the CIO approves, and no role transports in the last three days of a quarter.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT Fix forward quickly in production, or rebuild through the controlled route under pressure? The controlled route took longer but left nothing for the auditors to find.
WHAT I LEARNED The worst day of the project was caused by skipping the step we had spent six months building. The lesson was not new; the decision was.

blocks.text: Discussion
1. What check would have caught the master role change before 13:20?
2. Was Priya, not IT, the right person to extend the posting window? Why?

sections.title: Chapter 12 — What I Would Do Again

blocks.text: Chapter 12 — What I Would Do Again

By the end of September six of our twelve measures met target. SAP_ALL holders, generic IDs, leaver timeliness, firefighter reviews, direct assignments and provisioning speed were all where they should be. Conflicts, false positives, legacy roles and unused access were moving but not fast enough, SSO was close, and the quarter ended with a P1.

I would again start with the problem everyone knew and let its owner lead the fix. I would again write every decision down. I would add a deputy for the GRC administrator in the first month, not the fifth. And I would put the quarter-end freeze in place in March, not after it had cost us a day.

rows: WHAT I LEARNED A security lead earns trust by making the controlled way the easy way, by reporting numbers that are true even when they are bad, and by deciding in writing.

blocks.text: Discussion
1. Which of the six unmet measures would you put first in Q4, and why?
2. What would you hand over to a successor on 1 October?

sections.title: 1. The Role of the Security Lead

blocks.text: 1. The Role of the Security Lead

The Security Lead owns the access outcome of the programme: who can do what, how that is decided, and how it is proved. The lead sits between three groups that each think they own access: the business (role owners), IT (Basis and security administration) and assurance (the controls team and the auditors). The lead's value is making those three agree.

rows: Access design standards, the GRC set-up decisions, access reviews, incident command for access, the security metrics and decisions

THE THREE RULES OF THE ROLE Make the right thing the easy thing: if the controlled route is slower than the workaround, people will use the workaround. Measure access in numbers with a target, never in adjectives. Decide in writing: every design choice with a consequence gets an ADR.

blocks.text: 2. Designing the Workstream Team
Corvane's security workstream had six people, two of them shared. Organise them in three small pods with a lead each, and name a deputy for every person who is a single point of failure.

blocks.text: The shared GRC administrator is the workstream's biggest key-person risk. In May the workflow stall (INC-04) and the silent connector failure (INC-03) landed on the same person within a fortnight. Cross-train security analyst 2 on connectors and workflow monitoring in the first month.

blocks.text: Module 12 — Planning and Estimating a Security and GRC Workstream

Six sessions, about seven hours. By the end you can size a security workstream from its drivers, sequence it around the controls calendar and the quarter-ends, staff it without a single point of failure, write the conditions that protect it, and assemble the planning pack that is scored in the course. The module quiz is practice only; the planning pack is scored (20 percent of the course).

blocks.text: Security effort is driven by what must be designed, fixed, reviewed and run: users, roles, rules, emergency access, connected systems, identity and cloud systems, access deficiencies and review campaigns. Unlike a controls project, a security workstream usually has a fixed window set by the audit calendar, so the question is often not "how long?" but "how many people for this window?"

readings.title: TIB Security Workstream Estimating Model — Instructions

blocks.text: TIB SYSTEMS LLC | From SAP Project Manager to GRC and Security Lead
Security Workstream Estimating Model
Purpose

A driver-based model that sizes the effort of an SAP security and GRC workstream from counts of users, roles, rules, connected systems, identity and cloud systems, access deficiencies and review campaigns, and turns it into the team needed for a planned window or the duration for a planned team. It is calibrated so that the Corvane Energy Group security workstream (9 March to 30 September 2026) reproduces its actual capacity: 6 FTE for 29 weeks at 80 percent, 696 person-days.
How to use it
1. Inputs tab: enter your project in column D. Column B is the Corvane calibration; column C is the Redwater planning-pack brief from Module 12.
2. Factors tab: unit efforts per driver and the complexity multipliers. Replace them with your own history as soon as you have it.
3. Estimate tab: effort by work package, total effort, the team needed for your window, the duration with your planned team, and four checks.
Colour legend
Yellow with blue text = input. Grey = formula. Do not overwrite grey cells.
Important limits

The factors are illustrative planning assumptions calibrated to one fictitious case, not industry benchmarks. Present results as a range, state the assumptions, and agree the engagement conditions (Module 12, Session 12.5) before committing to a date. The model does not include project management of the wider programme, licence or infrastructure work, or GRC upgrades.

1. The Role of the Lead

You are the person who owns the outcome. You do not own the workbooks, the tests or the findings: your team does. You own four things: the scope and its defence, the team and its capacity, the relationship with every stakeholder who can help or hinder, and the conclusion that goes to the client. This playbook shows how one lead did that for a 15-person team on a US-listed oil and gas company, and turns it into reusable routines.

rows: How you know it is working
Every gate passes on its stated date with the Checks tabs reading ALL CHECKS PASS
Pod leads make decisions without escalating; you review conclusions, not drafts
No stakeholder first hears a finding in writing
Every number can be traced to a workbook row

THE LEAD'S THREE RULES 1. Nothing is a surprise.  Findings are spoken before they are written. 2. Nothing is sampled, filed or closed without a check.  Population passes IPE before sampling; evidence has an ID before it counts; retest passes before a deficiency closes. 3. Everything is traceable.  Any conclusion can be followed back to a server, and any server forward to a conclusion.

blocks.text: 4.2 Communication principles
Speak before you write. For any finding, meet the owner first with the evidence on the table.
One page per audience. The CFO gets decisions; process owners get what they must do; the auditors get attributes, populations and reliance decisions.
Lead with what works. Report effective controls first so the client knows what to protect.
State the denominator. "Thirty logged, nine open" always, never "70 percent".
Keep a decision log. Every steering decision is dated, owned and recorded.
4.3 Difficult conversations

rows: Telling the CIO that nine dialog users hold SAP_ALL
Meet in person; bring the usage analysis; separate the facts from blame
"Here is what we found, here is what these users actually did, and here is what I suggest we do together."
A defensive technical owner won't share extracts
Ask them to teach you how it works; make them a co-owner of the fix
"Show me how this runs today in your words; I will write it down before I judge it."
Telling the CFO nine deficiencies stay open

Prologue — The Phone Call

The call came on a Tuesday in early December. Eleanor Whitcombe, the CFO of Corvane Energy Group, did not waste words. "Our auditors have told us that our SAP controls are our biggest risk going into the next audit cycle," she said. "We moved to S/4HANA last year. We have a management letter with three IT points, an internal audit list of forty open findings, and a board that wants to hear the word remediated. Can you lead this?"

Corvane is an integrated oil and gas company: upstream fields offshore and onshore, a pipeline business, a refinery and a marketing arm, four company codes, joint venture partners in most of its assets, and a US listing that makes it subject to Sarbanes-Oxley. It runs one S/4HANA production system for all four company codes, with GRC for access, a Fiori front end, BW for consolidation, a cloud integration platform for banks and partners, and Solution Manager for change.

I had spent thirty-odd years in SAP security and controls work. I knew what a project like this looked like when it went well and, more often, when it did not. The failures had a pattern. Teams jumped to testing before they agreed what was in scope. They tested what was easy instead of what mattered. They found problems, wrote long reports, and left the client with a list instead of a result.

I told Eleanor I would take it on under three conditions: a named executive sponsor who would attend a steering committee every two weeks, read-only access for my team to every system in scope, and a rule that we would measure success by how many issues were actually closed, not how many we found. She said yes to all three before I had finished the sentence.

This is the story of what happened next: how I built the team, how we built the foundation, what we found, what it took to fix it, and why thirty deficiencies became nine. I have written it for the person who will lead the next project like this. I will tell you what I decided, why, and where I got it wrong.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT The sponsor, access and measure-of-success conditions were agreed before the contract was signed. A lead who negotiates these later will negotiate them from a weaker position, with a team already waiting.
WHAT I LEARNED Agree how success is measured on day zero. "Issues closed" is a different project from "issues found".

blocks.text: Questions for the new lead
What three conditions would you set before accepting a similar engagement?
How would you define "success" in numbers for your client?

sections.title: Chapter 1 — Week One: Listening Before Planning

blocks.text: Chapter 1 — Week One: Listening Before Planning
I started on 12 January 2026. My first week had no workbooks in it at all. I spent it with people.

I met the CFO, the CIO Raymond Okafor, the Group Financial Controller Priya Raman, the head of Internal Audit Martin Kessler, and Sofia Lindqvist, the external audit partner. I asked each of them the same four questions. What worries you most? What have you already tried? What would make this project a success in your eyes? What must I not do?

The answers were consistent in a way that surprised me. Eleanor wanted a clean opinion and no surprises. Raymond wanted his IT team treated as partners, not suspects. Priya wanted the controls to be simple enough for her accountants to operate. Martin wanted an audit trail he could rely on. Sofia wanted one thing above all: evidence that the automated controls could be trusted, so her team could rely on them and reduce their own testing.

Raymond's answer to "what must I not do" stayed with me. "Do not email my Basis lead a list of his failures," he said. Viktor Hale, the Basis Lead, had run the S/4HANA upgrade the previous year, and everyone knew some shortcuts had been taken to meet the go-live date. Viktor was proud and tired and, I would learn, frightened of what we would find.

I wrote down the project in one page: scope in plain words, the nine stages and gates from the foundation manual, the dates I could commit to, and the one measure. Then I took it to the first steering committee and asked everyone in the room to sign it. Not because the signature mattered, but because reading it aloud made people argue about scope on day five instead of week twelve. The CFO challenged whether joint venture accounting belonged in scope. I said yes, because JV receivables, payables and revenue share were all significant accounts. She agreed. That argument, early and cheap, saved us from a far more expensive one later.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT I chose a listening week over a planning week. The project plan I wrote on Friday was better than the one I would have written on Monday, and the stakeholders felt heard before anything had been tested.
WHAT I LEARNED The same four questions to every senior stakeholder gives you a map of conflicting priorities. Write it down before you design anything.

blocks.text: Questions for the new lead
Whose answer in your first week is most likely to change your plan?
What would you ask the Basis lead that is not an accusation?

sections.title: Chapter 2 — Building a Team of Fifteen

blocks.text: Chapter 2 — Building a Team of Fifteen

The budget gave me fifteen people. It sounds like plenty. It is not, for a landscape with eleven systems and four company codes. The real question was how to organise them so that no one waited for anyone and no work was done twice.

I split the team into four pods plus two cross-cutting roles, each with a lead who could make decisions without me. The Security and GRC pod: Tunde Adeyemi as lead, Lerato Dlamini on segregation of duties, and Samuel Boateng as tester. The ITGC pod for change and operations: Mei Lin as lead, Ivan Petrov as Basis consultant, and Elena Rossi as tester. The finance controls pod: Carlos Mendes as lead, with process analysts Fatima Khan for procure-to-pay, Arjun Mehta for order-to-cash and JV accounting, and Grace Liu for record-to-report, fixed assets and projects, plus Kofi Mensah as the tester for automated and business-process controls. The data and evidence pod: Nadia Haddad as data and IPE analyst and Olivia Grant as evidence coordinator. Across all of them, Hannah Brooks ran the programme office and Ruth Abara was our training and change champion.

Three design choices mattered. First, every pod had its own tester, and testers never reviewed their own work. Reviews went to the pod lead, and the pod leads' work came to me. Second, Nadia and Olivia sat in the middle of everything: nothing was sampled until Nadia had passed the population, and nothing was filed until Olivia had indexed it. That one rule is why we never had a sampling argument with the auditors. Third, Ruth joined on day one rather than at the end. She wrote the plain-language guides to each control as we designed it, so that by the time we reached remediation, the client's people had already read about what they would be asked to do.

My own role was narrower than I expected. I did not build workbooks. I removed obstacles, made the scoping decisions, ran the steering committee, and read every deficiency before it went to a client. In the first month I made the mistake of reviewing too much. By the second month the pod leads were reviewing each other's work, and I focused on conversations with the client.

The rhythm we kept for thirty-seven weeks was simple: a fifteen-minute stand-up each morning, a pod review each Wednesday, a one-to-one with each pod lead each week, a client sync on Thursdays, steering every second Friday. When a meeting stopped producing decisions, I cancelled it.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT I gave each pod a lead with decision rights rather than managing fifteen people directly. The cost was less visibility of detail; the gain was speed. I replaced detail with the Checks tabs: every workbook told me its own status.
WHAT I LEARNED A team of fifteen needs four conversations, not fifteen. Design the pods first and the individual roles second.

blocks.text: Questions for the new lead
How would you organise fifteen people across the nine stages of the foundation?
Which two roles would you put in the middle so nothing is sampled or filed unchecked?
Chapter 3 — Mapping the People

I treat stakeholders as a landscape of their own. Before the first workbook, I drew a map: who decides, who influences, who is affected, and who might quietly stop us. Over thirty-seven weeks the names did not change, but my view of them did.

The sponsor was Eleanor, and her job was to unblock. I never asked her for anything I could get elsewhere. When I did ask, it was for a decision, and I came with a recommendation and two options. Raymond, the CIO, was the owner of the systems and the people whose controls we would test. I made a rule early: findings about his team went to him in person before they went in writing. Priya, the Group Financial Controller, was the person who would operate most of the finance controls after we left, so I treated her as the customer of everything we designed.

Martin Kessler in Internal Audit was both a stakeholder and a risk. If we found things he had missed, he might feel exposed. I invited him to every gate review and shared the coverage matrix openly. He became the most useful challenger on the project. Sofia Lindqvist, the external audit partner, I treated as a user of our output from the first week: I asked what test attributes and sample sizes her team would accept, and I wrote them into the plan.

The process owners were the heart of the work: Beth Calloway in accounts payable, Jorge Salinas in procurement, Aiko Tanaka in treasury, Samira Qureshi for joint ventures, Derek Owusu in commercial, Liam Doherty for capital projects, Rosa Delgado in supply chain, Claire Foster in HR. Each one owned risks. Each one was busy. The best approach was a single twenty-minute walkthrough in their own office, with a one-page summary afterwards, not a workshop in a conference room.

The hardest relationship was Viktor Hale, the Basis Lead. Every finding in change management, privileged access and operations touched his team. In week two he told me, quietly, that he would give us whatever we asked for but he did not expect to enjoy it. I took that as an invitation. I made Mei and Ivan his working partners, not his auditors. We asked his team to show us how the landscape really worked, in their own words, and we wrote it down before we judged it. When the findings came, Viktor had already seen most of the evidence and had already started to fix it.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT I decided that nobody would learn about a finding in a report. Every finding was spoken first, to the person who owned it, with the evidence in front of both of us. It cost hours. It saved the project.
WHAT I LEARNED Name the one stakeholder who can stop the project without saying so. Make them your partner before the first finding.

blocks.text: Questions for the new lead
Which stakeholder would you meet in person before a written finding goes out?
How would you involve a defensive technical owner without lowering your standards?

sections.title: Chapter 4 — The Landscape: What We Found in Seven Weeks

blocks.text: Chapter 4 — The Landscape: What We Found in Seven Weeks

The first two gates were about facts, not controls. By 6 February we had to have every system and interface listed and validated; by 20 February, every process mapped to its systems and its financial statement accounts. This is the work nobody finds exciting and everything later depends on.

W01 started with the landscape diagram Viktor's team gave us, which showed eight systems. We finished with eleven. The differences were instructive. A Fiori front-end server was not on the diagram; we asked whether it posted transactions, and the answer was yes, for invoice entry and journals, so it came into scope. A sandbox existed that nobody had mentioned; we checked the transport route display and confirmed it had no path to quality or production, and we excluded it, with the screenshot as evidence. A training client was in the quality system; we confirmed it used masked data and excluded it. A cloud integration tenant carried every bank file and partner statement; the provider had a SOC 1 Type II report, which we obtained and later mapped to our own controls. And the database layer, the HANA database underneath the SAP system, had a SYSTEM user and a handful of administrators who could change financial tables without ever logging into SAP.

W02, the interfaces, was where the project's best early finding came from. We asked process owners what came into SAP from outside and what went out, and we asked each one how they would know if it failed. For the payment file sent to the banks, the answer was a pause and then: "I suppose treasury would notice if the bank complained." We checked the file directory. Four accounts payable users had write access to it. A payment file is a list of who gets paid and how much; anyone who could edit it could redirect money. That was in week three, long before any test. It became risk R-P2P-006.

Other interfaces told similar stories. The daily production volumes from the field allocation system fed revenue directly, and nobody reconciled what arrived to what was sent. The ChaRM connector between Solution Manager and production logged on with a user that held SAP_ALL. A custom upload program, ZFI_JE_UPLOAD, let twelve finance users load journals in bulk with no validation and no error log.

W03 settled the shape of the work: fourteen business processes plus four technical areas for access, change, operations and the database. We mapped thirteen financial statement line items to those processes. Payroll was the one process with no clear scope; Claire Foster confirmed in week three that payroll runs externally and SAP only receives the posting journal. Instead of guessing, we had marked it Outstanding until she said so, and it went in as a small, well-scoped interface.
We passed gate G1 on 6 February and G2 on 20 February. I did not feel any pride. I felt relief, because the scope was now written down and signed.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT I refused to start risk work until every system was either validated with evidence or flagged with an open question. The pressure to move on was strong in week four. I held the line because every risk, control and test later would point back to a system ID, and an unvalidated system is a hole in the foundation.
WHAT I LEARNED A landscape diagram is a claim, not a fact. Validate every row. Ask "how would you know if it failed?" of every interface. The answers are the risk register.

blocks.text: Questions for the new lead
Which system on a client's diagram would you want to validate first, and with what evidence?
What would you ask a payment-file owner to find out if the file can be altered?

sections.title: Chapter 5 — Risks, Controls and the Argument About "Control Areas"

blocks.text: Chapter 5 — Risks, Controls and the Argument About "Control Areas"

By March we turned to the risk register, the risk and control matrix, and the segregation-of-duties rules. This is where the foundation either becomes a controls project or stays a list of technical settings.

We wrote thirty-six risks, thirty-two of them relevant to SOX. Every risk followed the same sentence: there is a risk that something happens because of a cause, resulting in an impact. Writing them that way forced the process owners to say what could go wrong in words a tester could check. Beth Calloway in accounts payable had told me she had "no risks", only controls. After an hour we had seven, including the one she had been worrying about for years, vendor bank-detail changes made to divert payments.

Then came the argument I had expected. The client's existing control documentation listed what it called control areas: User Access, Change Management, Segregation of Duties. Internal Audit wanted to keep them as the unit of testing. I said no. An area is not a control. A control is one person or system doing one thing, at a stated frequency, producing evidence. I asked each owner to describe their control in five parts: who, what, when, how, and what evidence results. Forty-seven controls came out of that exercise, thirty-eight of them key controls. Some owners found out that what they thought was a control was actually a hope.

The matrix also taught us something I now put on the first slide of every kickoff: each control belongs to one category, not three. A three-way match is an automated application control. The control that stops someone changing the match tolerances is a change-management general control. SOX relevance is a flag that decides whether we test it, not another category. Understanding that let us build the reliance links: for every automated control and every report, we recorded which general controls it depended on. There were sixty-one such links.

The segregation-of-duties work belonged to Lerato and Tunde. We turned each risk into functions, transactions and authorisation objects: twenty functions and sixteen conflict rules, including the oil-and-gas-specific ones for joint venture equity changes and billing. We found four critical rules that could not be mitigated and had to be removed. Starting from the TIB baseline ruleset and adding the client's custom transactions got us to an approved version 1.0 on 27 March, gate G4.

By 10 April, gate G5, every one of the forty-seven controls had a named owner, a performer, an evidence owner and a backup. That list of names was the quiet achievement of the project. When we later asked for evidence, we never had to ask who to ask.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT When Internal Audit asked to keep control areas as the unit of testing, I offered a trade: keep the areas as a way to group, but test controls. They accepted because I showed them one control from their own documentation that nobody could describe in five parts.

WHAT I LEARNED A risk you cannot test is not a risk statement; a control you cannot evidence is not a control. The reliance links between general controls and automated controls are the most valuable thing in the matrix.

blocks.text: Questions for the new lead
How would you explain the difference between a control area and a control to a process owner?
Which stakeholder would you ask to approve the SoD ruleset, and why?
Chapter 6 — The Evidence Chase

Evidence is where good plans go to die. By June we had 95 requests to manage and a client team that was also running a quarter-end close. Olivia Grant ran the register like an air-traffic controller: every request had a control, a period, an owner, a due date and a status, and nothing was marked received until it had an evidence ID.

We organised requests in waves. Wave one asked for configuration and scoping evidence, twenty-two requests. Wave two asked for the complete populations, such as every SAP user, every leaver, every transport imported to production, every Firefighter session: twenty-eight requests. Wave three, twenty-five requests, asked for supporting evidence, but only for the items we had selected. Asking for a sample before you have a population is the quickest way to be accused of cherry-picking.

Nadia Haddad's completeness and accuracy checks caught three things that would have embarrassed us. The first extract of SAP users left out locked accounts, which would have hidden exactly the leavers we were looking for. The first export of transports covered sixty days instead of five months. And in the Firefighter log, three sessions appeared in the system security log but not in GRC, which meant someone had used an emergency ID outside the tool. We sent each extract back, explained the gap, and did not sample until the result was Pass.

These were the moments that built trust with the client's Basis team. We never said "your extract was wrong". We said "the parameters we captured show a filter on active users; can we rerun with all user types?" Viktor's analysts started checking their own extracts before sending them.
In the end we filed 109 evidence items and ran 45 checks of populations. Every conclusion we later wrote could be traced to an evidence ID, a request, and a control.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT I made it a rule that no sample is drawn from a population that has not passed its check. A manager asked me to relax it to save a week. I told him I would give him the week back later, and we gave it back by not having a single disputed sample.
WHAT I LEARNED Population first, sample second, evidence third. Nadia's completeness checks saved us more time than any other single step.

blocks.text: Questions for the new lead
Which populations would you check first on a similar project?
How would you tell a client their extract is incomplete without blaming them?
Chapter 7 — Testing: General Controls First

We finalised the test plan on 22 May. For each of the thirty-eight key controls there were two tests: a walkthrough of how the control is designed and a test of whether it operated. Seventy-six tests in all, each with written attributes derived from the control description, a sample size taken from the guide, a tester and a different reviewer.

The one planning decision I fought for was the order. General controls first, automated controls second. The reason is the reliance link. A three-way match that passes a test of one tells you the tolerances are right today. To say they were right all year, you need the change-management and access controls around them to have worked, or you need other evidence that nobody touched the configuration. Sofia's team needed that answer. So the access and change tests ran from 15 June to 10 July, and the automated-control tests from 13 July.

Each tester followed the same seven moves: read the control, walk it through, secure the population, select the sample, request the evidence, test every attribute, and conclude. I made Samuel, Elena and Kofi practise on a dummy control before the real tests, then insisted on a short peer review at the end of every workpaper. Not because they were weak, but because the first workpaper from any tester is always the one with a gap.

The easiest-looking tests were the most revealing. For the leavers test, we started from the HR report, not from the SAP lock list. Starting from SAP would only have shown us the users who were removed. For the transports test we started from what production received, not the list of tickets. For the access review we tested the listing the reviewers saw before we tested their decisions. In each case the start point was the system of record, because that is the only place a bypass shows up.
By 31 July every operating test was done. We had a pile of exceptions and no idea yet what they meant.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT I put the general controls ahead of the automated controls and kept the schedule even when the finance pod complained that they were idle for three weeks. Their idle weeks became their review weeks, and the reliance conclusions were all the stronger.

WHAT I LEARNED Start every test from the system of record, not from the process that is supposed to produce the record. Two tests per key control: design first. If the design is wrong, operating effectiveness is academic.

blocks.text: Questions for the new lead
How would you explain the order of tests to a finance team waiting to start?
What would be your system of record for a leavers test, a change test and a payment test?
Chapter 8 — What the Tests Found

The numbers were uncomfortable. Of the thirty-eight key controls, we had exceptions on twenty-three operating tests, two of them ineffective, and four design failures. Behind those numbers were stories.

Privileged access was the first. Nine dialog users, people who log on every day, held SAP_ALL, the profile that bypasses every authorisation check. Four generic IDs were active. The person who owned the monthly review had left in January and nobody replaced them. Tunde asked the most useful question of the project: "What have these users done?" Ivan pulled the transaction statistics and the change documents for each of the nine for the whole period. Display transactions, mostly. Two had changed document header texts. None had touched configuration or master data. That analysis would later decide whether the finding was a material weakness or a significant deficiency.

Fourteen role assignments had been made directly in the user maintenance transactions by Basis users, outside the GRC workflow. On two dates, production had been opened for changes without a ticket, and in the first window two Z-tables were changed. The pattern pointed to one origin: the 2025 upgrade, when the team had needed fast access, never withdrew it.

In the payment process, three weaknesses lined up. Sixty-one users had unmitigated critical segregation conflicts, including the ability to create a vendor and pay it. Six of twenty-five vendor bank-detail changes had no call-back to the vendor. Four AP users could write to the payment file directory. Any one would have been a finding. Together they described an open door.

Elsewhere the exceptions were smaller but telling. Six of twenty-five leavers were locked late, because the HR report reached Security weekly. A custom report built for the purchase-order exception review silently excluded orders marked for deletion, which meant thirty-one same-user purchase and receipt exceptions worth USD 210,000 were invisible to the reviewer. Eighteen EDI order messages sat in error for over a month, USD 84,000 of unbilled sales. And several reviews were late or thin: journals, bank reconciliations, JV statements, a BW consolidation load.

There was also good news, and I made sure the team and the client heard it. The access review, the backup process, the direct-change restrictions, the integration provider's SOC 1 report and seven of the key automated controls tested effective. The three-way match, posting-period control, depreciation configuration and journal-release workflow were sound. We had found a landscape with serious but concentrated weaknesses, not a landscape in disrepair.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT I presented the good results first at the steering committee. Not to soften what followed, but because Eleanor needed to know what could be relied on before she heard what could not.

WHAT I LEARNED Always ask "what have these users done?". Usage analysis is what turns a scary configuration finding into a measured one. Report what is working. The client needs to know what to protect.

blocks.text: Questions for the new lead
