sections.title: Chapter 9 — The Hard Week: Deciding What It Meant

blocks.text: Chapter 9 — The Hard Week: Deciding What It Meant
3 August was the hardest day of the project. We had thirty deficiencies and twenty-seven failed tests, and the next ten days decided how the client and the auditors would see them.

A deficiency is not an exception. Every exception goes through a path: is it real, is it design or operating, does it exceed the tolerated number in the sample, what could go wrong, what else compensates, and does it connect to others. We ran each one past that path with the pod leads, and discarded none. Then Carlos and I did the part nobody enjoys: grouping.

DEF-001, the nine SAP_ALL users, looked on its own like a moderate finding. But it shared a cause, a team and a time with the direct role assignments, the two production openings, the late Firefighter reviews and the missing role-owner approvals. They all pointed at the same event: the upgrade. Grouped, they described a team that could bypass access and change controls at will. We rated the group a significant deficiency. The deciding factor in not rating it a material weakness was the evidence: full-period change logs for the automated-control tables showed no unauthorised change, and usage analysis for the privileged users showed no misuse.

The second group was the payment process: unmitigated critical conflicts, weak bank-change verification, an unprotected payment file. Compensating controls existed but two of them were themselves deficient. We rated it a significant deficiency too, and before we did, Fatima and Kofi examined every vendor bank change and every payment run for the period. They found nothing improper. That substantive review is why I could tell the CFO the exposure was theoretical, not actual.

The conversation with Eleanor was short. I did not bring slides. I brought the coverage matrix and two sheets of paper, one for each group. I said what we found, what we did to measure the impact, what we recommended, and what the auditors were likely to think. She asked one question: "Can this be fixed before year end?" I said yes for twenty-one of the thirty, and told her honestly which nine would need longer and why. She did not argue.

The reliance decisions came next. For each of the twelve automated controls, the two report controls and the review controls that depend on reports, we asked three questions. Could the configuration have changed without authorisation? Could the control have been overridden? If so, could we show with other evidence that it did not happen? Of sixty-one dependency links, eleven were fully supported because the general control around them was effective, forty-nine were supported with documented additional procedures, and one, the payment-file integrity control, was not relied on for the period. Sofia's team accepted our reasoning and tested the configuration themselves only for the nine tables we had flagged.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT I decided to group the findings before I presented any of them. Presented individually, thirty findings would have made Corvane look like it had no controls. Presented as seven groups with causes, they looked like what they were: a few concentrated failures with identifiable origins, and a long tail of small ones.

WHAT I LEARNED Do the follow-up work before the severity discussion. The usage analysis and the substantive review changed the answer from "possible material weakness" to "significant deficiency, no loss". Group by cause. A client can fix a cause; they cannot fix thirty items.

blocks.text: Questions for the new lead
What follow-up evidence would you gather before rating a privileged-access finding?
How would you decide whether three weaknesses on one fraud scenario are one finding or three?

sections.title: Chapter 10 — Remediation: Turning Findings into Fixes

blocks.text: Chapter 10 — Remediation: Turning Findings into Fixes

A finding that is not fixed is only a report. I wanted every deficiency to have an owner, a date and a fix that addressed the cause, not just the instance. Removing SAP_ALL from nine users fixes nine users. Preventing Basis from assigning roles without a request, and alerting when production opens, fixes the cause.

We wrote the remediation plans with the owners, not for them. Tunde sat with Neil Abernathy, the IT Security Manager, and agreed that SAP_ALL would exist only on Firefighter IDs, that Basis would lose user and role maintenance rights, and that GRC would alert on any direct assignment. Mei and Viktor agreed that opening production would trigger an automatic alert to the CIO and to me. Aiko in treasury restricted the payment directory to the integration service account and Yuki, the integration lead, added a hash check that alerted if the file the bank received differed from the file SAP created.

Some fixes were technical, some were behavioural. The late Firefighter reviews were fixed with a reminder at day three and an escalation at day five. The missing bank-change call-backs were fixed by removing the "urgent" path altogether. The HR leavers lag disappeared when Claire Foster agreed to send a daily feed into GRC that locks the account automatically. The purchase-order report was corrected and moved under change control, with a checklist for every report used in a key control.

I insisted on three rules. Every remediation date fell before the retest, never after. Every owner got a one-page plain-language guide from Ruth describing what they were agreeing to do. And I told the steering committee that a deficiency would be closed only when a retest showed the new control operating, not when someone told me it was done.

The remediation window ran from August to September. We had underestimated one thing: how many occurrences a control needs before a retest is meaningful. A weekly control needs about five weeks. A monthly control needs two month-ends. A quarterly control needs two quarters. We worked back from the retest dates and moved the implementation dates for weekly and daily controls forward by a week, and for the rest we agreed in advance with the auditors that a short operating period would leave the deficiency open.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT I let the retest calendar set the remediation deadlines, not the other way round. It made the plan harder to agree and made the results harder to argue with.
WHAT I LEARNED Fix the cause, not the instance. Write the plan with the owner, in their language. Know how many occurrences each control needs before you promise a retest date.

blocks.text: Questions for the new lead
How would you decide which fixes to agree first?
How would you explain to a CFO why a monthly control cannot be retested after three weeks?

sections.title: Chapter 11 — Retest, Results and the Nine That Stayed Open

blocks.text: Chapter 11 — Retest, Results and the Nine That Stayed Open
The retests ran from 7 to 25 September. By the end, nineteen retests were done and every one was effective, closing twenty-one deficiencies, including both significant-deficiency groups.

The results are in the workbooks, but here they are in plain terms. Nine dialog users with SAP_ALL became none: SAP_ALL now exists only on Firefighter IDs. Fourteen direct role assignments in five months became zero among 188 assignments since remediation. Sixty-one users with unmitigated critical conflicts became none. Six late leaver locks out of twenty-five became none out of twenty-five. Six bank changes without a call-back out of twenty-five became none. Four people with write access to the payment file directory became one service account, and the hash alert caught a test alteration within minutes. Eighteen aged EDI order errors became none. Two unapproved openings of production became none.

Nine deficiencies stayed open, all at the lowest severity and none material. Five were quarterly or monthly controls that need more operating cycles: the quarterly database administrator review and the monthly reviews for journals, bank reconciliations, JV statements and the BW load. One was the emergency-transport approval, which cannot be tested until there is an emergency. Two were design fixes still in progress: the redesigned volume reconciliation and the locked depletion input file. One was a single AUC settlement documentation gap that needs the next qualifying settlements. I told the steering committee exactly which retest would close each one, and on what date.

Thirty became nine. That is a seventy percent reduction. I kept repeating the denominator, because a number without a base invites argument. Thirty deficiencies were logged in the baseline cycle. Twenty-one were closed after a retest showed the new control operating. Nine remain, with owners and due dates between 27 November and 18 December. And the severity of what is left is a fraction of what we started with: two significant-deficiency groups became none, and there is no material weakness.

There was a second result that mattered as much. The auditors relied on the automated controls. Sofia confirmed in writing that for the period, the three-way match, posting-period control, depreciation configuration, journal-release workflow and the others could be relied upon, supported by the general controls and the additional procedures we had documented. Her team's own testing of IT-dependent areas shrank accordingly.

I did not claim victory. The nine open deficiencies are real. But on 30 September 2026 the coverage dashboard read: every risk covered, every key control tested, every deficiency evaluated, every exception traced to a deficiency, and a conclusion of no material weakness and no significant deficiency.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT I gave the steering committee a one-page close-out with a table of what was fixed, a table of what was open and when each would close, and the thirty-to-nine headline with its base. I deliberately resisted rounding the story up.

WHAT I LEARNED Always state the denominator. "Seventy percent fewer" needs "of thirty, logged in the baseline cycle". Say plainly what is still open and when it closes. Credibility is made in the last meeting.

blocks.text: Questions for the new lead
How would you present partial success to a board that wants a clean result?
What would you do about an open deficiency that depends on an event that may not happen soon?

sections.title: Chapter 12 — Handover and What I Would Do Differently

blocks.text: Chapter 12 — Handover and What I Would Do Differently

A controls project that ends when the consultants leave has not ended. In the last month we handed the workbooks to Priya's team and Ruth ran four half-day sessions for the control owners, one for each pod's area. We left a monthly dashboard that reads the same coverage checks, a quarterly calendar for the access review and the DBA review, and a plain list of the nine open items with their retest dates. Priya's deputy now owns the foundation workbooks. Martin's team uses them for its own audits.
I learned a great deal and some of it the hard way.

I would have asked for the HR leavers feed in the first month, not the fifth. A daily feed is a quick technical fix that would have prevented one of the deficiencies, and I knew the weekly report was a problem from the first walkthrough. I did not raise it because I wanted to be sure. I should have raised it and been wrong.

I would have scheduled the weekly-control fixes earlier. The nine open deficiencies are partly an honest outcome and partly a result of my own calendar. If I had pulled the weekly and monthly remediation dates forward by three weeks, at least two of them would have closed.
I would have involved Internal Audit in the design of the remediation, not just the testing. Martin's team had ideas I only heard in the lessons-learned session.
I would have taken the fifteen-person team to the client's site for one week together in the first month. The pods worked well, but the project was strongest in the week the whole team shared a room.

And I would have said no more often. At least twice I accepted requests for extra testing that were interesting but outside the scope we had signed. Each time the cost was a week of one pod's time and no change in what the client knew.

If you are the next lead, here is what I would tell you in one paragraph. Build the foundation before you test anything. Make the thread from landscape to conclusion traceable in both directions. Hold the line on the population before the sample. Test general controls first. Group findings by cause. Talk to people before you write to them. Fix causes, not instances. Do not close anything without a retest. Say what is still open. And care about the people on your team and your client's team, because in thirty-seven weeks they are the project.

rows: LEAD'S DECISION POINT The last decision I made was to leave the workbooks with the client and not take a copy for ourselves. A controls project that produces a dependency on its consultants has failed on its own terms.
WHAT I LEARNED The measure of the project is the state of the client when you leave, not the report you hand over.

sections.title: Module 1 — Controls and Audit for the SAP Project Manager

blocks.text: Module 1 — Controls and Audit for the SAP Project Manager

Module 1 has six short sessions, about seven hours in all. Each has outcomes, an explanation, an example from the Corvane case, a "PM lens" that compares the idea with project management, an exercise and three questions. A quiz and an answer key close the module.

rows: What the auditor needs from you

blocks.text: Session 1.1 — Why Controls Projects Exist

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Explain internal control over financial reporting in plain language. Say who does what: management, internal audit, external audit and the audit committee. State what a controls project delivers and to whom.

blocks.text: 1.1.1 The problem

The financial statements of a listed company are produced largely by systems. If the systems post a wrong number, or let someone post a number they should not, the statements are wrong. The company has to show that it has designed and operates controls that would prevent or detect such errors in time. When a company is subject to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) in the United States, management must assess and report on the effectiveness of its internal control over financial reporting, and the external auditor of larger companies must also give an opinion on it. Other countries have similar regimes. The rules depend on the company's listing and size, so on a real project always confirm the requirement with the client's finance and audit teams.
1.1.2 The four parties

rows: What they want from a controls project
Owns the controls and must assess them
A defensible assessment and no surprises
Independent assurance for management and the audit committee
An audit trail they can rely on and reuse
Audits the statements; for larger companies, also opines on internal control
Evidence that automated controls and reports can be relied on, so they can reduce their own testing
Oversees reporting and audit for the board
A clear picture of what is fixed, what is open and how serious it is

blocks.text: 1.1.3 What a controls project is

A controls project builds and proves the foundation for that assessment. It identifies the systems and processes that matter, states the risks, defines the controls that answer them, tests whether those controls are designed well and operate, evaluates what fails, and helps fix and retest it. Its output is not a long report but a result the client can defend: what is covered, what was tested, what failed, what was fixed and what remains.

rows: IN THE CORVANE CASE Corvane Energy Group is a US-listed oil and gas company with one production S/4HANA system for four company codes. Its CFO, Eleanor Whitcombe, sponsored the project; Internal Audit and the external audit partner were stakeholders from week one. The project ran for 38 calendar weeks and ended with 30 deficiencies logged, 21 closed after a retest and 9 open, no material weakness.
PM LENS A controls project has a normal project life cycle, but its deliverable is evidence. A late milestone can be recovered; an unsupported conclusion cannot.
TRY IT 1.1 In your own words, write two sentences each on what the Corvane project delivers to (a) the CFO, (b) the external audit partner and (c) the head of Internal Audit.

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. Who owns the controls: management, internal audit or the external auditor?
2. Why does the external auditor care whether automated controls can be relied on?
3. What is the difference between the output of an audit and the output of a controls project?

rows: KEY POINTS Management owns the controls and must assess them; auditors give independent assurance. A controls project builds the foundation for that assessment. Its deliverable is a defensible result, not a report.

blocks.text: Session 1.2 — The Vocabulary of Controls

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Define risk, control, assertion, key control, preventive and detective. Write a control in five parts. Classify a control by nature and frequency.

blocks.text: 1.2.1 Risk and control

A risk is something that could go wrong and cause the financial statements to be misstated, written as: there is a risk that something happens because of a cause, resulting in an impact. A control is one person or system doing one thing, at a stated frequency, producing evidence, that prevents or detects the risk. One risk can need several controls; one control can answer several risks.
1.2.2 Assertions

An assertion is a claim the financial statements make: that transactions occurred (occurrence), nothing is missing (completeness), amounts are right (accuracy), they are in the right period (cut-off), balances exist (existence) and are valued correctly (valuation). Each risk is tied to the assertions it threatens.
1.2.3 Kinds of control

rows: Stops the error happening; finds it after it happens
The system does it; a person does it using a system report; a person does it without a system
Continuous, event-driven, daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, annual
How often it operates; frequency drives sample size
Relied on to address a SOX-relevant risk; key controls are formally tested

blocks.text: 1.2.4 The five-part description

A good control description answers five questions: who performs it, what they do, when or how often, how (system, report or criteria), and what evidence results. If you cannot say what evidence it produces, it is not yet a control.

rows: The IT Security Administrator (who) locks and end-dates the SAP user of every leaver (what) within two business days of the HR termination date (when), using the daily HR leavers report and SU01 or GRC (how). Evidence is the leavers report annotated with lock dates and the SU01 change history.

The AP Analyst (who) verifies every vendor bank-detail change by calling the vendor on an independently sourced number before the change is saved (what) for every change (when) using the call-back procedure and log (how). Evidence is the call-back log with approver.

IN THE CORVANE CASE The risk "a fictitious vendor is created and paid" (R-P2P-001) is answered by several controls: the segregation-of-duties analysis (C-ITGC-SOD-001), the weekly vendor change review (C-BPC-P2P-001) and the call-back control (C-BPC-P2P-002). The first removes the conflict, the others detect or prevent misuse. None of them alone covers the risk.
PM LENS A control is like a task in a plan: it has an owner, a frequency and an output. A control with no evidence is like a milestone with no deliverable.

TRY IT 1.2 A.  Rewrite each in five parts, inventing sensible details: "Access is reviewed regularly." and "The system checks invoices."  B.  For each of these, say whether it is preventive or detective and automated, IT-dependent manual or manual: (i) the system blocks an invoice outside the price tolerance; (ii) the controller reviews a report of large journals each month; (iii) the AP analyst phones the vendor before changing bank details.

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. What are the five parts of a control description?
2. Which is typically tested more often: a daily control or an annual control, and why?
3. What makes a control "key"?

rows: KEY POINTS Risk: what could go wrong. Control: who does what, when, how and with what evidence. Assertions say what the risk threatens. Frequency drives the sample size.

sections.title: Session 1.3 — IT Controls in Three Layers

blocks.text: Session 1.3 — IT Controls in Three Layers

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Distinguish ITGCs, ITACs and IT-dependent manual controls with reports (IPE). Explain why general controls protect automated controls. Read a reliance decision.

blocks.text: 1.3.1 Three layers

rows: The environment that all automated controls and reports depend on: access, change, operations (and, when a project is in the period, development)
User provisioning, leaver removal, access reviews, privileged and Firefighter access, transports, production change settings, job and interface monitoring, backup
Automated controls built into SAP configuration
Three-way match tolerances, duplicate invoice check, posting periods, release strategies, depreciation keys
ITDM and IPE: IT-dependent manual controls and information produced by the entity
Controls performed by people using a system report; the report itself must be complete and accurate
The controller's review of a report of large journals; a BW reconciliation report

blocks.text: 1.3.2 The four ITGC domains

rows: Who can get in, and what can they do?
How does a change reach production, and who approves it?
Do jobs, interfaces and backups run and get fixed when they fail?
Were new implementations and migrations controlled? (relevant only when one is in the period)

blocks.text: 1.3.3 Reliance: why ITGCs protect ITACs

An automated control such as the three-way match is only a setting in a table. A test of it shows the setting is right today. To say it was right all year, you need the change and access controls around it to have worked, or other evidence that nobody changed it. That dependency is called reliance. If a general control fails, the automated control is not automatically wrong, but the presumption of reliance is gone and extra procedures are needed.

rows: IN THE CORVANE CASE C-ITAC-001, the three-way match, relies on three general controls: transports (C-ITGC-PC-001), system and client settings (C-ITGC-PC-002) and privileged access (C-ITGC-AC-005). All three had exceptions, so reliance was recorded as "supported with additional procedures": a full-period review of table change logs and of the transports that touch the tolerance tables, and a usage analysis of the users who held SAP_ALL. The auditors accepted the reliance.
PM LENS Think of the ITGCs as the platform and the ITACs as the workloads running on it. If the platform is unmanaged, you cannot vouch for the workloads without extra checks.

TRY IT 1.3 A.  Classify each as ITGC, ITAC, ITDM or manual business-process control: (i) password length parameter; (ii) three-way match; (iii) quarterly user access review; (iv) AP supervisor's weekly review of the vendor change report; (v) call-back to the vendor before a bank change; (vi) transport approval; (vii) daily batch job monitoring; (viii) monthly reconciliation of BW to the ledger.  B.  The transport approval control failed. What does that do to your reliance on the three-way match, and what would you do?

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. Name the three ITGC domains that are tested on almost every project.
2. Why is a test of one enough for an automated control?
3. What does "supported with additional procedures" mean?

rows: KEY POINTS ITGCs are the environment; ITACs are settings; ITDMs are people using reports. Reliance links the layers. A failed ITGC removes the presumption of reliance; other evidence can restore it.

blocks.text: Session 1.4 — How Controls Are Tested

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Explain the test of design and the test of operating effectiveness. Choose a population, attributes and a sample for a simple control. Name the four kinds of test procedure.

blocks.text: 1.4.1 Two tests per key control

rows: If performed as described, would this control address the risk?
Did the control actually operate throughout the period?
Walkthrough of one instance with the performer
Inspection or reperformance of a sample across the period
The control has a design deficiency
The control has an operating deficiency

blocks.text: 1.4.2 Procedures

rows: Weakest alone; never sufficient by itself
Good for a moment in time
Examine documents, records or system output

blocks.text: 1.4.3 Population, sample and attributes
Population: the complete list of items the control applies to for the period (all leavers, all transports imported, all payment runs). It must be complete and accurate: that is the IPE check.

Sample: items drawn from the population. Sample size depends on how often the control operates. Typical practice: 25 to 60 for event-driven controls, 20 to 40 for daily, 5 to 15 for weekly, 2 to 5 for monthly, 2 for quarterly, 1 for annual. Follow the auditor's methodology where there is one.
Attributes: the conditions each item must meet to count as a pass, written from the control description.
Evidence: what you obtain to prove each attribute.

rows: IN THE CORVANE CASE For C-ITGC-AC-002 (leavers locked within two business days) the population was the HR leavers report, 214 leavers from 1 January to 31 May 2026, not the list of locked SAP users. Starting from SAP would only have shown users who were removed. The sample was 25. The attributes were: A the leaver is on the HR report; B the user is locked or end-dated; C the lock is within two business days of termination; D there is no logon after termination. Six of 25 were locked late, because the HR report reached Security weekly, and one had a display-only logon.

CORE INSIGHT — START FROM THE SYSTEM OF RECORD The population for a test comes from the authoritative source for the thing being controlled: HR for leavers, what production received for changes. Starting from the process that is supposed to produce the record can never find a bypass.
PM LENS A population is like the complete work breakdown structure: if it is incomplete, no sample from it tells you about the whole.

TRY IT 1.4 For the control "every vendor bank-detail change is verified by a call-back before it is saved":  A.  What is the population and where does it come from?  B.  Write four attributes.  C.  The control is event-driven: what sample size range is typical?  D.  Name one procedure that is stronger than inquiry and say how you would use it.

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. What is the difference between a population and a sample?
2. Why is inquiry never enough on its own?
3. Why must a population be checked before sampling?

rows: KEY POINTS Two tests per key control: design, then operating. Population, sample, attributes and evidence are the four building blocks. Start from the system of record.

blocks.text: Session 1.5 — Deficiencies and Severity

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Tell an exception from a deficiency. Use the three severity levels. Explain grouping, compensating controls, remediation and retest.

blocks.text: 1.5.1 From exception to deficiency

An exception is a fact: a sample item did not meet an attribute. A deficiency is a judgement: the control, as designed or as it operated, does not let management prevent or detect misstatements on a timely basis. Between the two sits an evaluation: is the exception real, is it a design or an operating failure, is the number of failures above what the sample tolerates, what could go wrong, what else compensates, and does it connect to other findings.
1.5.2 Three levels of severity

rows: The control does not allow management or employees to prevent or detect misstatements on a timely basis
Less severe than a material weakness but important enough to merit the attention of those overseeing financial reporting
There is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the financial statements will not be prevented or detected on a timely basis

blocks.text: Severity depends on how large the potential misstatement is, how likely it is, whether fraud is possible, whether other controls compensate, and, for general controls, whether automated controls and reports that depend on them can still be relied on.
1.5.3 Group by cause
Thirty separate findings overwhelm a client. Group them by cause and process and evaluate the group. Several modest deficiencies with one cause can together be significant.
1.5.4 Remediation and retest

Every deficiency needs an owner, a date and a fix that addresses the cause, not only the instance. A deficiency is closed only when a retest shows the remediated control operating. How long a retest needs depends on the control: roughly five weeks for a weekly control, two month-ends for a monthly one, two quarters for a quarterly one.

rows: IN THE CORVANE CASE Corvane logged 30 deficiencies in seven groups. Group A, privileged access governance, included nine dialog users with SAP_ALL, 14 role assignments made outside GRC, two openings of production without a ticket and late Firefighter reviews. Usage analysis showed no misuse, so it was rated a significant deficiency, not a material weakness. Group B, the payment process, combined conflicting access, weak bank-change verification and an unprotected payment file; a review of every bank change and payment run found nothing improper, and it too was rated significant. After remediation and retest, 21 deficiencies were closed and nine remained open, all at the lowest severity.

PM LENS Evaluation is like impact assessment of a project risk: probability, impact, mitigation and the combined effect of related risks, with the difference that the standard you are held to is set by the auditor.

TRY IT 1.5 A client has these facts: (i) nine dialog users hold SAP_ALL; (ii) usage analysis shows they only displayed data; (iii) 14 role assignments were made outside the request workflow; (iv) production was opened twice for changes without a ticket.  A.  Should you treat these as four findings or one group, and why?  B.  What would make you rate the group a material weakness?  C.  What would you need to see in a retest before closing it?

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. What is the difference between an exception and a deficiency?
2. Name the three severity levels in order.
3. Why is a deficiency closed only after a retest?

rows: KEY POINTS An exception is a fact; a deficiency is a judgement. Group by cause, then rate the group. Close only on a retest.

sections.title: Session 1.6 — What the Auditor Needs from You

blocks.text: Session 1.6 — What the Auditor Needs from You

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES List what an external auditor needs from a controls project. Prepare the first conversation with the audit partner.

blocks.text: 1.6.1 The auditor's view

External auditors may use the work of management and internal audit if it is reliable. The more it can be relied on, the less the auditors need to test again themselves. They look for four things: clear scope that ties to the significant accounts, evidence that is complete and traceable, tests designed to the auditor's own standards of attribute and sample, and an honest evaluation with the denominator stated.
1.6.2 The week-one conversation
On a controls project the single most useful conversation in week one is with the audit partner. Agree what they will accept before you test. Questions to ask:
Which significant accounts and processes do you consider in scope, and what materiality do you use?
What test attributes and sample sizes will you accept for each type of control?
What do you need to rely on automated controls, and which general controls do you expect to see tested?
What operating period do you need after a fix before you will accept a retest?
How will you classify and aggregate deficiencies, and when do you want to hear about a possible significant deficiency?
What are your timing constraints and which evidence format do you prefer?

rows: IN THE CORVANE CASE At Corvane the lead asked the external audit partner in week one which attributes and sample sizes she would accept and wrote them into the plan. In week 34 he agreed the retest sample sizes and operating periods with her before issuing the evidence requests. In week 31 the auditors accepted 49 reliance decisions with additional procedures, 11 fully supported, and 1 not relied on.
PM LENS This is stakeholder requirements gathering with an unusually clear customer: the auditor tells you the acceptance criteria. Ask before you build.
TRY IT 1.6 You are about to meet the external audit partner of a new oil and gas client. List your five most important questions and, for each, say what you will do with the answer.

blocks.text: Check yourself
1. Why does the auditor care how reliable management's work is?
2. What is the benefit of agreeing sample sizes in week one?
3. Who should hear about a possible significant deficiency first, and why?

rows: KEY POINTS The auditor can rely on your work only if it is complete, traceable and tested to their standard. Agree attributes, samples and operating periods before you test. Tell the client first; no surprises.

6. What is a key control?
7. Name the three layers of IT controls.
8. Name the three main ITGC domains.
9. Explain "reliance" in one sentence.
10. What is the difference between a test of design and a test of operating effectiveness?
11. Why must a population be complete?
12. Name the four test procedures from weakest to strongest.
13. What is the difference between an exception and a deficiency?

Quiz answers

There is a risk that [event] because [cause], resulting in [impact]
A claim the financial statements make, such as occurrence, completeness, accuracy, cut-off, existence or valuation

Session 1.1

Model answers. (a) CFO: a defensible assessment of internal control and a clear statement of what is fixed and what is open, with no surprises. (b) External audit partner: evidence that automated controls and reports can be relied on, tested to their standards, so their own testing can be reduced. (c) Head of Internal Audit: a complete audit trail and a foundation they can reuse in their own audits. Check yourself: (1) Management. (2) Because reliance reduces how much they must test themselves. (3) An audit gives an opinion on the statements; a controls project builds and proves the foundation for management's assessment.
Session 1.2

The system (who) blocks payment of any vendor invoice outside the tolerance limits for price, quantity and receipt (what) at every invoice posting (when), comparing purchase order, receipt and invoice (how). Evidence is the tolerance configuration and the blocked-invoice records.
Detective; IT-dependent manual (a person using a report)

blocks.text: Check yourself: (1) Who, what, when or how often, how, evidence. (2) A daily control, because there are many more occurrences, so the sample is larger. (3) It is relied on to address a SOX-relevant risk.

ITDM (a manual control that relies on a system report)

The presumption of reliance on the three-way match is gone. Do extra work: review the change log of the tolerance tables for the full period, inspect any transports touching them, and analyse who could change the settings, then document whether reliance is still supported

(3) The general control had exceptions, but other documented procedures show the configuration did not change, so the automated control can still be relied on.

rows: All vendor bank-detail changes in the period, from the change documents in SAP (for example table CDPOS), reconciled to the call-back log
A call-back log entry exists; the number called was independently sourced; the call was made and approved before the change was saved; the change agrees to the request
Inspection (examine the log entry and the change request) or reperformance (re-contact a vendor from the independent number to confirm)

blocks.text: Check yourself: (1) A population is everything the control applies to; a sample is the part you test. (2) Because the performer may be mistaken or may overstate what happens; it needs corroboration. (3) A sample from an incomplete population says nothing about what is missing.
Session 1.5

rows: One group. The four facts share a cause (access and change rights granted during an upgrade and never withdrawn) and one team. Together they describe a team that can bypass access and change controls; each fact alone understates that

Evidence of misuse (for example changes to configuration or master data by the privileged users), or no way to show that automated controls and reports were not altered, so reliance cannot be restored

New controls operating for long enough: no SAP_ALL on dialog users, no role assignments outside the workflow, an alert on every production opening, and a sample of recent events passing the same attributes

blocks.text: Check yourself: (1) An exception is a fact about an item; a deficiency is a judgement about the control. (2) Control deficiency, significant deficiency, material weakness. (3) Because only a retest shows the remediated control operating.
Session 1.6

Model answer: use the six questions in 1.6.2. For example, "What sample sizes will you accept?" tells you whether to follow the standard guide or the auditor's own; "What operating period do you need after a fix?" tells you when to schedule retests; "When do you want to hear about a possible significant deficiency?" tells you how to plan escalation. Check yourself: (1) Because the less they can rely on, the more they must test themselves. (2) It avoids rework and disagreement at the end. (3) The client (the CFO and the CIO for matters touching IT), in person, because no one should learn of a finding from a report.

sections.title: Session 17 — How Part 3 Uses the Foundation

blocks.text: Session 17 — How Part 3 Uses the Foundation
17.1 From workbook to test

Parts 1 and 2 built the foundation. Part 3 uses it. Every test in this part starts from a row in the Test Plan (W10), which was generated from a key control in the RCM (W05), which responds to a risk in the Risk Register (W04), which belongs to a process or technical area in W03 running on a system in W01. Each session below names that thread at the top so the trainee never loses sight of why the test is being performed.
SYS → BP → RISK → CTRL → TEST → POPULATION (EV, IPE) → SAMPLE (SMP) → ATTRIBUTES → RESULT → DEF
17.2 The universal test cycle
Every access, change, operations and ITAC test in Parts 3A and 3B follows the same seven moves. Learn them once; the control areas only change the data sources.

rows: Re-read the five-part control description and the risk it addresses
Follow one instance end to end with the performer; confirm the design would address the risk
Obtain the full population for the period and complete the IPE check
Select by the approved method, across the whole period
Raise wave 3 PBC requests for the selected items
Complete the attribute grid; reference an EV-ID for every tick or exception
Record the result in W10; raise DEF-IDs in W13; update reliance in W05 and W14

sections.title: 17.3 Access controls in scope for Part 3A

blocks.text: 17.3 Access controls in scope for Part 3A

rows: C-ITGC-AC-005 Privileged, generic and default IDs

blocks.text: C-ITGC-AC-005, C-ITGC-AC-006 and R-TECH-005 ("unauthorised users gain access through privileged, default or weakly protected accounts") are held at source in W04 and W05 (Part 1, Sessions 5 and 6, and the key register). Following Session 16.4, new keys are always created at source, never only in a workpaper.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — ACCESS TESTS ARE POPULATION TESTS Most access failures are found not in the sample but in the population: an active user with no HR record, a dialog user holding SAP_ALL, a Firefighter ID left unlocked. Always analyse the full population first, then test the sample. A clean sample over a dirty population is a wrong conclusion.

blocks.text: Session 18 — WP-AC-01 User Provisioning

rows: C-ITGC-AC-001 — New and changed access is requested and approved by the line manager and role owner in GRC ARM, with SoD analysis, before provisioning to ECP/300
SYS-03 / SYS-04 → BP-TECH-01 → R-TECH-001 → C-ITGC-AC-001 → C-ITGC-AC-001-TOE

blocks.text: 18.1 What the control must achieve

Only access that a business owner has approved for a business reason should ever reach production. The control must ensure three things: approval happens before access is granted, the approver has the authority to approve that role, and what was granted matches what was approved. Where GRC is used, the request also passes an SoD check so conflicts are seen before they are created.
18.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: Access Management > Access Request (NWBC/Fiori); report: Access Request Details / Approver Delegation
Request, approvers, approval timestamps, SoD result, provisioning log
Who created users / assigned roles, and when
Table AGR_USERS (via SE16 display or SUIM RSUSR002)
Current roles per user with valid-from/to dates
User type, creation date, creator (ANAME), validity
GRC Access Control > Master Data > Role (Business Role Management) or client role-owner list
Who is authorised to approve each role

blocks.text: 18.3 Population and IPE

The population is every user created and every role assignment added in ECP/300 during the test period. Extract it from RSUSR100N (change documents for users, role assignments) with the period dates, or from the GRC request report filtered to provisioned requests. EV-031 contains 214 new role assignments across 61 users from 01-Jan to 30-Sep.

IPE (IPE-004): screenshot of RSUSR100N selection parameters (client 300, full date range, no user filter); total count reconciled to GRC provisioning log count plus assignments made outside GRC; five assignments traced both ways between file and AGR_USERS. Any assignment made outside GRC, for example directly in PFCG or SU01 by Basis, is itself a potential exception and must be kept in the population, not filtered out.
18.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Walk through one new-joiner request with the GRC administrator: request created, manager approval, role owner approval, SoD analysis, automatic provisioning.
Confirm the workflow cannot be bypassed: who can assign roles directly in SU01/PFCG in production (holders of S_USER_GRP and S_USER_AGR with change activity)?
Confirm role owners are defined for every role in scope.
Conclude whether the design addresses R-TECH-001 and R-P2P-001.
18.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: A documented access request exists for the assignment
Approved by the line manager before provisioning
Approval timestamp vs AGR_USERS / RSUSR100N date
Approved by the authorised role owner before provisioning
Roles provisioned agree to roles approved
SoD analysis run; any conflict mitigated or rejected
GRC risk analysis result; mitigation ID

blocks.text: 18.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — Read C-ITGC-AC-001 and R-TECH-001 in W05/W04. Confirm IPE-004 = Pass.
Step 2 — Analyse the full population: flag assignments with no GRC request number and assignments made by Basis users directly. These are investigated regardless of the sample.
Step 3 — Select 25 assignments (event-driven guide) by seeded random selection across all three quarters; log as SMP-005.
Step 4 — Raise PBC-044 for GRC request records for the 25 items.
Step 5 — For each item, complete attributes A–E. Compare timestamps to the minute where the system allows.
Step 6 — Document exceptions with cause from inquiry; record result in W10.
18.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing
Population analysis found 6 assignments without a GRC request, all made by Basis user BASIS_ADM via SU01 on 14-Mar.

rows: Role owner approval missing: approved by line manager only
Population exception: direct SU01 assignment, no request

blocks.text: Result: Exception noted. One sample deviation (item 7) and six population exceptions. Inquiry shows the six assignments were an urgent month-end fix without a later retrospective approval. These are raised together as DEF-006 and evaluated in W13, including whether any of the six users performed transactions with the access (STAD / change documents).
18.8 Evaluating exceptions
A missing approval is a deviation even if the access looks appropriate; the control is about approval, not suitability.
Approval after provisioning is a deviation. Record the gap in days.
Population exceptions (bypass of the workflow) usually weigh more than sample exceptions, because they show the control can be avoided.
Check whether the users holding direct-assignment rights (S_USER_GRP/S_USER_AGR) is itself a W06 sensitive-access item.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — TEST THE BYPASS, NOT JUST THE WORKFLOW GRC workflows almost always work as configured. The real risk is the path around them: Basis or security staff assigning roles directly in production. The population analysis in step 2 is what finds it.

blocks.text: Session 19 — WP-AC-02 Termination of Leavers

rows: C-ITGC-AC-002 — The IT Security Administrator locks and end-dates SAP users within two business days of the HR termination date

blocks.text: 19.1 What the control must achieve

A leaver who keeps an active SAP account can still post or approve transactions, either personally or through someone who knows the password. The control must remove the ability to log on promptly, and the test must show not only that accounts were locked but that no one used them after the termination date.
19.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: HR system (SuccessFactors / HCM PA40 actions / external HR)
Authoritative list of terminations and dates
USR02 fields UFLAG (lock), GLTGB (valid to), TRDAT/LTIME (last logon)
Lock status, end date, last logon
Date and time the user was locked and by whom

blocks.text: 19.3 Population and IPE

The population is the HR leavers list for the period, not the SAP lock list. Starting from SAP would only show the users that were removed and miss those that were not. EV-021 contains 48 leavers from 01-Jan to 30-Sep. IPE-003: count reconciled to the HR headcount movement report; five leavers traced to HR personnel records.

Before sampling, match all 48 leavers to USR02 using the HR employee ID to SAP user mapping (often USR21 / the user's personnel number). Any leaver whose account is still unlocked and valid at the extraction date is a population exception.
19.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Walk through one termination: HR action, notification to IT Security, lock in SU01/GRC, confirmation.
Confirm how IT Security is notified (automatic feed, weekly report, email) and what happens to leavers with no SAP account.
Confirm the mapping between HR employee and SAP user is maintained.
19.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: Leaver appears on the HR leavers report with termination date
SAP user is locked or end-dated
Lock or end date is within two business days of termination
No logon after the termination date

blocks.text: 19.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — Confirm IPE-003 = Pass and agree the user-mapping approach with Basis.
Step 2 — Match all 48 leavers to USR02; flag unlocked accounts and logons after termination for the whole population.
Step 3 — Select 25 leavers across the period (SMP-006).
Step 4 — Obtain RSUSR100N lock events for the 25 users (PBC-045).
Step 5 — Complete attributes A–D; calculate business days between termination and lock.
Step 6 — Investigate any post-termination logon through SM20/STAD to see what was done.
19.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing

rows: 14 business days; logon on 10-Mar (display only, SM20)

blocks.text: Result: Exception noted, 3 of 25. Cause: the HR leavers report is sent weekly rather than daily. This becomes DEF-004 (worked in Part 2, Session 14.4). Compensating control C-ITGC-AC-003 (quarterly review) was tested effective.
19.8 Evaluating exceptions
Late removal without use is a deviation in timeliness; late removal with use raises severity and needs activity analysis.
A leaver with no SAP account is not an exception, but keep the evidence of the match.
Contractors and agency staff often fall outside the HR report; ask how they are terminated and test them separately if material.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — START FROM HR, NOT FROM SAP The population for a leaver test always comes from the authoritative source of terminations. A list of locked SAP users can only ever show the control working.

sections.title: Session 20 — WP-AC-03 Periodic User Access Review

blocks.text: Session 20 — WP-AC-03 Periodic User Access Review

rows: C-ITGC-AC-003 — Quarterly, role owners review all users and their roles in ECP/300 through GRC UAR; inappropriate access is removed within 10 business days

blocks.text: 20.1 What the control must achieve

Provisioning and termination controls deal with individual events; the access review catches what they miss: role creep, transfers, and accounts that should have been removed. The control is only as good as the list it reviews and the care of the reviewer, so the test focuses on completeness of the review population, precision of review, and follow-through on removals.
20.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: Access Control > Access Request > User Access Review; reports: UAR Review Status, Request status
The user/role listing generated for the campaign
AGR_USERS, USR02 at campaign generation date
GRC removal requests; RSUSR100N role removal dates

blocks.text: 20.3 Population and IPE

There are two populations. First, the reviews themselves: 3 quarterly campaigns in the period (Q1–Q3), each with role-owner review packages. Second, within each sampled campaign, the user/role lines reviewed. Quarterly frequency gives a sample of 2 campaigns.

IPE is critical here and is tested under C-IPE-001 and recorded in the dependency tab: the campaign listing must contain every active user and role assignment at the generation date. Reconcile the campaign line count to AGR_USERS for active users at that date.
20.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Walk through one campaign: generation, distribution to reviewers, decisions, escalation, closure.
Confirm reviewers are the role owners (or line managers) defined in W07, not the users themselves.
Confirm reviewers see enough information (role description, sensitive access, SoD flags) to make a judgement.
20.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: Campaign listing is complete (reconciles to AGR_USERS at generation date)
Every package reviewed by an authorised reviewer
Review completed within the defined window
Reviewer evidence shows a real review (removals, comments or explicit confirmation of sensitive access)
Rejected access removed within 10 business days

blocks.text: 20.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — Select Q1 and Q3 campaigns (SMP-007).
Step 2 — For each, reconcile the listing to AGR_USERS at the generation date (attribute A).
Step 3 — Confirm every package was completed by an authorised reviewer (B, C).
Step 4 — Select 10 reviewer packages and inspect decisions; challenge any package where every line was approved in seconds (D).
Step 5 — For every rejection in the sampled campaigns, trace the removal (E).
Step 6 — Cross-check: users found as exceptions in WP-AC-01 and WP-AC-02 — did the review catch them?
20.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing

rows: 4,812 lines reconciled; 37 rejections, all removed within 10 days
2 packages closed 9 days late after escalation; within tolerance per policy? — confirm with owner
JSMITH (WP-AC-02) was removed in the Q1 review — supports compensating-control conclusion

blocks.text: Result: Effective, pending confirmation of the late-completion tolerance with the control owner. The cross-check is what lets W13 treat C-ITGC-AC-003 as compensating for DEF-004.
20.8 Evaluating exceptions
A review based on an incomplete listing fails attribute A even if every reviewer did their job.
"Rubber-stamp" reviews (every line approved, no comments, completed in seconds) are a design and operating concern; discuss with the reviewer and document.
Rejected-but-not-removed access is a high-impact exception: the control detected the problem and then failed to fix it.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — THE LIST IS PART OF THE CONTROL A user access review relies on IPE. If the listing omits a user group (for example, users with roles assigned through composite roles or reference users), those users were never reviewed. Always test the listing before the review.

sections.title: Session 21 — WP-AC-04 Privileged, Generic and Default IDs

blocks.text: Session 21 — WP-AC-04 Privileged, Generic and Default IDs

rows: C-ITGC-AC-005 — Privileged authorisations (SAP_ALL, SAP_NEW, user admin, table change, debug-change) and generic/default IDs are restricted to approved users; default IDs are locked or secured; Basis reviews the list monthly
SYS-03 / SYS-06 → BP-TECH-01 → R-TECH-005 → C-ITGC-AC-005 → C-ITGC-AC-005-TOE

blocks.text: 21.1 What the control must achieve

Privileged access overrides every other control. A dialog user with SAP_ALL can create a vendor, pay it, and change the configuration that would have blocked it. Default IDs such as SAP* and DDIC are known to attackers. Generic IDs remove accountability. The control must keep this access small, approved and monitored, and the test examines both the current state and the monthly review over the period.
21.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: SUIM > Users by Complex Selection (RSUSR002), profile SAP_ALL / SAP_NEW
RSUSR002 with authorisation values (W06 Sensitive_Access list)
Holders of S_USER_GRP, S_TABU_DIS 02, S_DEVELOP 02 etc.
RSUSR003 (status of SAP*, DDIC, EARLYWATCH, TMSADM in all clients)
USR02 USTYP (A dialog, B system, C communication, S service, L reference)
Identifies technical IDs used for dialog logon
HANA: users with system privileges (via DBA cockpit / SQL by Basis)
Privileged access below the SAP layer (SYS-06)

blocks.text: 21.3 Population and IPE

This test combines a point-in-time analysis of the full user population (EV-012, IPE-001 Pass) with a test of the monthly review. The review population is 9 monthly reviews (Jan–Sep); the monthly guide gives a sample of 2–5, here 3 (SMP-008).
21.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Inspect the privileged-access policy and the approved holder list.
Walk through one monthly review: who generates the list, who reviews, what is done with unapproved holders.
Run RSUSR003 in every PRD client, including 000 and 066 if present.
21.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: Every holder of SAP_ALL / SAP_NEW / W06 sensitive items is on the approved list with a business reason
No dialog (type A) generic IDs without named ownership
Default users locked or with changed passwords in all clients
Monthly review performed, evidenced and acted upon (sampled months)

blocks.text: 21.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — Run the population analyses (A–C) on EV-012 and RSUSR003 output.
Step 2 — Extend to HANA (SYS-06) using the Basis-provided list of database users with system privileges.
Step 3 — For the 3 sampled months, inspect the review evidence and follow up actions (D).
Step 4 — Map every unapproved holder to W06 SENS-IDs and to the risks they create.
21.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing

rows: BASIS_ADM (approved, Basis lead) and FI_SUPPORT1 (not approved; dialog user)
All approved FF IDs — expected per W06 SENS-004
TRAINING01 in client 300, active, last logon 02-Jul
SAP* locked, DDIC password changed in all clients

blocks.text: Result: Ineffective. FI_SUPPORT1 holding SAP_ALL as a dialog user, an active generic ID in production, and a missing review month together form DEF-007. Because this control is a dependency for C-ITAC-004 and C-ITAC-005, W05 ITGC_Dependency and W14 ITGC_Reliance are updated, and additional procedures are required before relying on those ITACs (Part 3B).
21.8 Evaluating exceptions
Privileged access held by an unapproved dialog user is a significant exception even if never used; then test usage (SM20, STAD, change documents) to see whether it was.
Approved privileged access with no monitoring is a design gap, usually solved by moving it to Firefighter.
Always report the result to the Part 3B ITAC tests; this is the reliance link in action.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — ONE PRIVILEGED USER CAN UNDO THE AUDIT Privileged-access results flow into every ITAC and IPE that relies on this system. A single unapproved SAP_ALL holder means configuration may have been changed outside the change process, so reliance on automated controls must be re-examined.

blocks.text: Session 22 — WP-AC-05 Emergency Access (Firefighter)

rows: C-ITGC-AC-004 — Emergency access through GRC EAM Firefighter IDs is requested with a reason, approved before use, logged, and every log is reviewed by the assigned controller within five business days
SYS-04 → SYS-03 → BP-TECH-01 → R-TECH-002 → C-ITGC-AC-004 → C-ITGC-AC-004-TOE

blocks.text: 22.1 What the control must achieve

Firefighter IDs carry broad, sensitive access for urgent fixes. The control makes that access safe: it is borrowed only when needed, with a reason, by an authorised user, every action is logged, and an independent controller reviews what was done. The test checks the IDs themselves, the sessions, and the reviews.
22.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: GRC > Emergency Access Management > Firefighter IDs, Owners, Controllers, Firefighters
Who can use which FF ID; who reviews
AGR_USERS for each FF ID in ECP
What each FF ID can do
GRC EAM reports: Firefighter Log Summary, Consolidated Log Report, Transaction Log and Session Details
Every session, reason, transactions, change documents
GRC EAM log review requests / controller sign-off
USR02 for FF IDs (should be locked when not checked out, depending on configuration)

blocks.text: 22.3 Population and IPE

Population: every Firefighter session in the period from the Firefighter Log Summary (EV-034, 186 sessions). IPE-005: count reconciled to the Consolidated Log Report and to SM20 logons by FF IDs; five sessions traced both ways. A session in SM20 that is missing from the GRC log means the ID was used outside EAM and is a population exception.
22.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Inspect EAM configuration: FF IDs, assigned roles, owners, controllers, and whether log review workflow is active.
Walk through one session: request, approval, logon, actions, log, controller review.
Confirm a controller cannot review their own sessions and that firefighters cannot be their own controller.
22.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: Session has a reason code and description that matches the activity
Use was approved before the session (pre-assigned and authorised, or approved request)
Log reviewed by the assigned controller
Review completed within five business days
Activity was consistent with the stated reason; anomalies followed up

blocks.text: 22.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — Population analysis: compare SM20 logons by FF IDs with GRC sessions; confirm FF IDs are not used for direct logon.
Step 2 — Inspect FF ID role content against W06: are SoD-conflicting or SAP_ALL roles assigned, and is that approved?
Step 3 — Select 25 sessions (SMP-009), weighted to include sessions with change activity.
Step 4 — Complete A–E; for E, compare transactions executed to the reason given.
Step 5 — Record the result in W10 and update W14.
22.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing

rows: Reason "month-end"; activity included XK02 vendor bank change, not followed up

blocks.text: Result: Exception noted. Item 14 is the more serious: a vendor bank-detail change under a generic reason, reviewed and approved without query. It is raised as DEF-008 and the vendor change is referred to the P2P team to confirm the payment was legitimate. This is the thread working in both directions: an ITGC test produced a question for a business-process risk (R-P2P-001).
22.8 Evaluating exceptions
A late review is a timeliness deviation; a review that fails to question unusual activity is a precision deviation and is weighed more heavily.
Sessions outside EAM (SM20 logons not in GRC logs) mean the control can be bypassed and are always significant.
Check that FF IDs are not used for routine work; high session counts for the same task suggest a missing standard role.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — REVIEW THE ACTIVITY, NOT THE SIGNATURE A controller sign-off proves the log was opened, not that it was understood. Attribute E, comparing the transactions to the stated reason, is where Firefighter tests find their real exceptions.

sections.title: Session 23 — WP-AC-06 Segregation of Duties and Sensitive Access

blocks.text: Session 23 — WP-AC-06 Segregation of Duties and Sensitive Access

rows: C-ITGC-SOD-001 — GRC ARA risk analysis runs at provisioning and monthly at user level against the approved ruleset; conflicts are removed or assigned an approved mitigating control
ITGC-APD · IT-dependent manual · Event-driven and monthly
SYS-04 → SYS-03 → BP-P2P-01/03 → R-P2P-001 → SOD-001 → C-ITGC-SOD-001 → C-ITGC-SOD-001-TOE

blocks.text: 23.1 What the control must achieve

SoD prevents one person from controlling a transaction end to end. The W06 ruleset defines which combinations are not allowed. The control must detect every conflict that exists, and for each one either remove it or apply a mitigating control that is real and tested. The test reruns the analysis independently, then checks how each conflict was handled.
23.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: Access Risk Analysis > User Level, Permission level, Rule set = approved version (W06)
GRC > Mitigated Users; mitigating control master data
Which users have which mitigations, validity dates
RSUSR008_009_NEW (critical combinations) using W06 rules; or table analysis on AGR_USERS + AGR_1251
Whether conflicting access was actually used

blocks.text: 23.3 Population and IPE

Population: the full user population at period end (EV-012) run against the approved W06 ruleset, plus the monthly ARA results for the period. The tester either runs ARA themselves with the client (observed) or reruns the rules independently from AGR_USERS and AGR_1251 (EV-013). The independent run is the IPE test of the client's ARA report.
23.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Confirm the ruleset in GRC agrees to the W06 approved version (functions, actions, permissions, custom Z-transactions).
Walk through one provisioning request flagged with a conflict: was it rejected or mitigated, and by whom?
Inspect the mitigating controls in GRC: each must exist in W05 with an owner and test.
23.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: Independent analysis agrees to client ARA results (no unreported conflicts)
Each conflict is either removed or has an approved, valid mitigation
Mitigating control exists in W05 and was tested effective
Critical conflicts (SOD-001, SOD-003) have no unmitigated holders
Where unmitigated, usage of the conflicting access is analysed

blocks.text: 23.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — Run the independent analysis for SOD-001 to SOD-005 at permission level, applying the org-level logic from W06.
Step 2 — Reconcile to the client's ARA output; explain every difference (A).
Step 3 — For each conflicting user, test B–D; select 25 if the conflict population is large (SMP-010).
Step 4 — For unmitigated conflicts, analyse usage over the period (E).
Step 5 — Feed results to W13 and to the business-process risk owners.
23.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing

rows: FI_SUPPORT1 (via SAP_ALL), and two AP supervisors; one AP supervisor used both XK02 and F110 in the period

blocks.text: Result: Ineffective for SOD-001 and SOD-003. The AP supervisor's use of both vendor maintenance and payment is referred for a payment review over the period. Raised as DEF-009. FI_SUPPORT1 links this finding to DEF-007 (WP-AC-04); W13 evaluates them together because they share a root cause.
23.8 Evaluating exceptions
A conflict reported by transaction but not executable at permission level is a false positive; document the rationale and keep it in W11.
A mitigation that is assigned but untested, expired, or not in W05 does not mitigate.
Unmitigated critical conflicts with actual usage require analysis of the transactions performed, not just a statement that access existed.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — RERUN, DO NOT RECEIVE The client's ARA report is IPE. If the ruleset is incomplete or the report is filtered, it will under-report conflicts. Independent rerun of the rules against AGR_USERS and AGR_1251 is what gives the result its authority.

sections.title: Session 24 — WP-AC-07 Password and Logon Parameters

blocks.text: Session 24 — WP-AC-07 Password and Logon Parameters

rows: C-ITGC-AC-006 — SAP logon and password parameters in ECP are set in line with the ABC password policy on all application servers, and changes follow change management

blocks.text: 24.1 What the control must achieve

System parameters enforce the password policy automatically. Because it is configuration, the test is a test of one, with confirmation that the setting applied all period. Two traps catch trainees: parameters can differ between application servers, and Single Sign-On may mean SAP password settings are not the real control for most users.
24.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: RZ11 (single parameter) or report RSPARAM on each instance; SM51 to switch servers
RZ10 profile versions; SM21 system log for dynamic changes
Whether values changed in the period
SNC / SSO configuration (Basis); USR02 password status fields
Whether users log on by password or SSO

blocks.text: 24.3 Population and IPE

No sample. The population is the set of in-scope parameters on every application server in ECP (EV-015, RSPARAM output per server listed in W01 Server_Detail). Confirm that the server list agrees to SM51.
24.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Obtain the password policy and map each requirement to its parameter.
Confirm whether SSO is used and for which user groups; if so, also obtain evidence of the directory (e.g. Active Directory) policy.
Confirm how profile changes are controlled (link to C-ITGC-PC-001).
24.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: Values identical on all application servers and unchanged in period (or changed through change management)

blocks.text: 24.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — List all application servers from SM51 and confirm against W01.
Step 2 — Run RSPARAM on each server, or have Basis do so while observed; capture parameters A–E.
Step 3 — Compare to the policy and to each other server.
Step 4 — Inspect RZ10 profile version history for the period.
Step 5 — Conclude; where SSO is used, note that the directory policy is the effective control and test it or rely on another team's work.
24.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing

Result: Exception noted. The second application server allows 10 failed attempts because its instance profile overrides the default profile. Raised as DEF-010 (low severity, with change-management cause referred to Part 3B).
24.8 Evaluating exceptions
Always test every application server; an instance profile can override the default profile.
A value that meets policy today but changed during the period requires testing for the whole period.
If SSO is used for all dialog users, password parameters are a lower-weight control; say so in the conclusion.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — CONFIGURATION IS TESTED ONCE, BUT EVERYWHERE Automated controls need only a test of one, but "one" means one test of every place the configuration lives, plus evidence it did not change. That second part depends on Program Change ITGCs, the subject of Part 3B.

blocks.text: End of Part 3A

Part 3A tested the seven access control areas and raised DEF-006 to DEF-010, two of which (DEF-007 and DEF-009) affect reliance on automated controls. Part 3B continues with Program Change (transports, system and client settings, direct changes), Computer Operations (batch jobs, interfaces, backup), ITAC configuration testing with the reliance assessment, and IPE testing of key reports.
