Session 25 — Where Part 3B Picks Up
25.1 The story so far

Part 3A tested access. Two of its results matter for everything that follows: DEF-007 (an unapproved dialog user, FI_SUPPORT1, holding SAP_ALL) and DEF-009 (unmitigated vendor-maintenance and payment conflicts). Both mean someone could have changed data or configuration outside the normal controls. Part 3B tests the other ITGC domains, then brings all ITGC results together to decide whether the automated controls (ITACs) and system reports (IPE) can be relied on.

rows: C-ITGC-PC-002 System and client change settings
C-ITGC-PC-003 Direct changes and debugging in production
C-ITAC-004 Three-way match; C-ITAC-005 Posting periods
C-IPE-001 Key reports used in controls

blocks.text: C-ITGC-PC-003, C-ITGC-CO-002 (interfaces, separate from batch jobs in C-ITGC-CO-001), C-ITGC-CO-003, C-IPE-001 and R-TECH-006 ("financial data cannot be recovered after failure or corruption") are held at source in W04 and W05 (Part 1, Sessions 5 and 6, and the key register).

rows: CORE INSIGHT — CHANGE CONTROLS ARE THE GUARD ON CONFIGURATION An ITAC is only a setting in a table. Program Change ITGCs decide whether that setting could have moved during the year. Read every Part 3B change result with the question: could the three-way match or posting-period configuration have been altered without anyone knowing?

blocks.text: Session 26 — WP-PC-01 Transport Management

rows: C-ITGC-PC-001 — Every transport imported to ECP has an approved change ticket, evidence of testing and business sign-off in QAS, and is imported by Basis, not the developer; emergency changes are approved retrospectively within two business days
SYS-01 → SYS-02 → SYS-03 → BP-TECH-02 → R-TECH-003 → C-ITGC-PC-001 → C-ITGC-PC-001-TOE

blocks.text: 26.1 What the control must achieve

Transports are how programs and configuration reach production. The control must ensure that every change entering ECP was requested, approved, tested and moved by someone independent of the person who built it. The test starts from what actually arrived in production, never from the change tickets, because a ticket list cannot show a change that bypassed it.
26.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: STMS > Import Overview > ECP > Import History; table TPALOG
Every transport imported, date, time, return code, importing user
SE01 / table E070 (TRKORR, AS4USER owner, AS4DATE, TRSTATUS)
Who created and released the request
Table E071 / E071K (objects and table keys)
What changed: programs, configuration tables (e.g. T169G, T001B)
ITSM tool (ServiceNow / Jira) or SAP Solution Manager ChaRM
Who can import; are any developers among them
Confirms the DEV → QAS → PRD path

blocks.text: 26.3 Population and IPE

The population is every transport imported to ECP/300 in the period from TPALOG / STMS import history (EV-019, 312 transports; IPE-002 Pass). Do not use the ITSM change list: it can only show changes that went through ITSM.

Before sampling, analyse the full population: (1) match every transport to a ticket number (often in the request description); (2) compare E070 owner to the importing user; (3) flag imports with no prior import to QAS; (4) flag transports containing ITAC configuration tables (E071K for T169G, T001B, credit control tables), which are always selected.
26.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Walk through one normal and one emergency change from ticket to import.
Inspect the import-rights list: confirm developers cannot import to production.
Confirm the transport route forces QAS before PRD (no direct DEV → PRD route).
26.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: Approved change ticket exists before import to PRD
Evidence of testing in QAS and business sign-off
Imported by a user other than the request owner
Transport content agrees to the approved change
Emergency changes approved retrospectively within two business days

blocks.text: 26.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — Run the four population analyses above on EV-019.
Step 2 — Select 25 by seeded random selection (SMP-003), plus all transports touching ITAC tables (here 2), giving 27.
Step 3 — Raise PBC-040 for tickets and test evidence.
Step 4 — Complete A–E for each item.
Step 5 — Record the list of ITAC-table transports for Session 32.
26.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing

Population result: all 312 transports have ticket references; no developer imported to production. Sample result: Exception noted, 1 of 27 (missing test sign-off), raised as DEF-011, low severity. Both ITAC-table transports were approved and tested, which is direct evidence for Session 32.
26.8 Evaluating exceptions
A missing ticket for a transport is a population exception and is always significant: the change bypassed the process.
Developer importing their own change is a segregation failure; check the importing user against the developer list, not just the request owner.
Transports containing configuration for ITACs feed the reliance assessment whatever the result.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — START FROM PRODUCTION The change population comes from what production received (TPALOG), not from what the change process recorded. Only that direction can find a change that skipped the process.

sections.title: Session 27 — WP-PC-02 System and Client Change Settings

blocks.text: Session 27 — WP-PC-02 System and Client Change Settings

rows: C-ITGC-PC-002 — ECP is set to "Not modifiable" (SE06) and client 300 to "No changes allowed" for client-specific objects and no changes to cross-client objects (SCC4); any opening is approved, time-limited and logged; table logging is active
ITGC-PC · Automated (configuration) with manual opening process · Continuous

blocks.text: 27.1 What the control must achieve

If production is open for changes, configuration and repository objects can be changed directly, without a transport, so C-ITGC-PC-001 sees nothing. These settings keep production closed. The test confirms they are closed today, finds every time they were opened during the period, and checks that table logging is on, because Session 32 depends on those logs.
27.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: SE06 > System Change Option; Display Log
Global setting and history of openings
SCC4 > client 300 details; change documents for table T000 (via SCU3 if logged)
Client role, change and transport settings, history
Whether table changes in client 300 are logged in DBTABLOG
RSUSR002: S_ADMI_FCD, S_CTS_ADMI, S_TABU_CLI / SCC4 and SE06 rights

blocks.text: 27.3 Population and IPE
Configuration is tested once on every relevant setting. The openings are a population: every SE06 and SCC4 change in the period from the logs (EV-022: 3 openings). All are tested.
27.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Inspect the procedure for opening production (approval, duration, who closes it).
Confirm who holds the rights to change SE06 and SCC4.
Confirm rec/client includes 300 (or ALL) so table logging is active.
27.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: SCC4 client 300: No changes allowed; no changes to repository and cross-client customising; production role
Every opening had prior approval and a ticket
Every opening was closed within the approved window and changes made were reviewed
SE06/SCC4 log; DBTABLOG for the window

blocks.text: 27.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — Capture current settings (A, B) with date and system visible.
Step 2 — Run RSPARAM on each server for rec/client (C).
Step 3 — Extract SE06 and SCC4 change history for the period; list every opening.
Step 4 — Test D and E for all openings; for each window, list table changes made in DBTABLOG.
Step 5 — Pass the logging result and any open windows to Session 32.
27.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing

rows: No ticket; opened by BASIS_ADM; same day as direct SU01 assignments (DEF-006)

blocks.text: Result: Exception noted. The 14-Mar opening was unapproved. DBTABLOG for the window shows changes to two Z-tables but none to T169G or T001B. Raised as DEF-012 and linked to DEF-006 because the same user and date are involved. W13 will consider whether these share a root cause.
27.8 Evaluating exceptions
An unapproved opening is significant even if no changes are found, because it shows the control can be bypassed.
If rec/client is off, there is no evidence of direct table changes; that alone can prevent reliance on ITACs.
Always analyse what changed during an opening; a closed system today says nothing about the period.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — THE LOGS ARE PART OF THE CONTROL Table logging (rec/client) is what allows the tester to prove that ITAC configuration did not change during the year. Check it here, early, because Session 32 cannot be completed without it.

sections.title: Session 28 — WP-PC-03 Direct Changes and Debugging in Production

blocks.text: Session 28 — WP-PC-03 Direct Changes and Debugging in Production

rows: C-ITGC-PC-003 — Debug-with-change and direct table editing in ECP are restricted to Firefighter IDs; the Security Audit Log records these events and Basis reviews them monthly

blocks.text: 28.1 What the control must achieve

Even with production closed, a user with the right authorisation can change data in memory through the debugger or edit tables directly. These changes leave no transport and often no change document. The control restricts the ability and monitors its use.
28.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: RSUSR002: S_DEVELOP with OBJTYPE = DEBUG, ACTVT = 02
Who can change values in the debugger
RSUSR002: SE16N with &SAP_EDIT, S_TABU_DIS / S_TABU_NAM ACTVT 02
Whether debug and critical events are recorded for all users
Debugger change events and critical transactions

blocks.text: 28.3 Population and IPE

Two parts. Rights: the full user population (EV-012). Events: all debug-change and SE16N edit events for the period from the audit log and SE16N log (EV-024: 7 events). Monthly reviews: 9; sample 3 (SMP-011).
28.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Confirm the Security Audit Log is active with filters covering all users and clients for the relevant events.
Confirm the log retention covers the whole period.
Walk through one monthly review.
28.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: Only FF IDs hold debug-change and table-edit rights
Audit log active and filters cover required events for all users
Each event was performed under Firefighter with a valid reason

blocks.text: 28.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — Run the rights analysis (A). Reuse W06 SENS items.
Step 2 — Inspect audit log configuration and retention (B).
Step 3 — Match every event to a Firefighter session tested in WP-AC-05 (C).
Step 4 — Test the three sampled monthly reviews (D).
28.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing

rows: FI_SUPPORT1 holds S_DEVELOP DEBUG 02 through SAP_ALL (same as DEF-007)
All 7 under FF IDs with reasons; none by FI_SUPPORT1

blocks.text: Result: Exception noted on A only; no new deficiency raised because it is part of DEF-007. The fact that the audit log shows no debug-change events by FI_SUPPORT1 is recorded as evidence for Session 32.
28.8 Evaluating exceptions
Rights without use are still an exception against attribute A; usage analysis decides severity.
If the audit log is not active for all users, debug changes cannot be detected; treat this as a design gap.
Link findings to existing DEF-IDs rather than raising duplicates for the same root cause.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — ONE FINDING, MANY TESTS FI_SUPPORT1 appears in WP-AC-04, WP-AC-06 and WP-PC-03. The workbook set lets the tester record it once (DEF-007) and reference it everywhere, so the client sees one problem with its full impact.

blocks.text: Session 29 — WP-CO-01 Batch Job Monitoring

rows: C-ITGC-CO-001 — Critical financial batch jobs are scheduled under an approved technical user, monitored daily by Basis, and every failure is ticketed and resolved

blocks.text: 29.1 What the control must achieve

Many financial processes run in batch: payment runs, GR/IR clearing, depreciation, interface postings. If a critical job fails and nobody notices, transactions are incomplete. Jobs also run under a step user whose authorisations apply, so a job can be a route to privileged access.
29.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: SM37; tables TBTCO (header, status, scheduler) and TBTCP (steps, step user)
Client document; agreed with process owners
Who can schedule or change jobs, or run as other users

blocks.text: 29.3 Population and IPE

Daily monitoring over ~190 working days in the period; daily guide gives 25 days (SMP-012). Separately, all cancelled runs (status A) of critical jobs in the period from TBTCO (EV-026: 14) are tested in full.
29.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Inspect the critical job list and confirm it covers jobs for in-scope processes (F110 payment run, GR/IR, interface postings).
Walk through one day of monitoring and one failure ticket.
Inspect step users for critical jobs: technical user type B, not a dialog user; authorisations appropriate.
29.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: Monitoring performed and evidenced on the sampled day
Failure resolved and rerun with completeness confirmed
Critical jobs run under approved technical users

blocks.text: 29.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — Confirm the critical job list with process owners.
Step 2 — Test A for 25 sampled days.
Step 3 — Test B and C for all 14 cancelled runs.
Step 4 — Test D for all critical jobs.
29.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing

rows: All evidenced via daily SM37 checklist
13 ticketed and rerun; 1 GR/IR clearing failure on 30-Jun not ticketed, rerun 4 days later
F110 scheduled under dialog user AP_SUPER1, who is also in DEF-009

blocks.text: Result: Exception noted. Untracked failure (DEF-013, low) and the payment run scheduled under a dialog user who already has an unmitigated SoD conflict. The latter is added to DEF-009 as additional impact.
29.8 Evaluating exceptions
A job running under a dialog or privileged user is an access issue as well as an operations issue.
A failure that was rerun late may affect period-end cut-off; inform the R2R team.
If no critical job list exists, it is a design gap; agree one before testing operating effectiveness.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — JOBS CARRY THEIR USER'S ACCESS A batch job has every authorisation of its step user. Reviewing step users connects Computer Operations back to the access tests in Part 3A.

sections.title: Session 30 — WP-CO-02 Interface Monitoring and Reconciliation

blocks.text: Session 30 — WP-CO-02 Interface Monitoring and Reconciliation

rows: C-ITGC-CO-002 — Errors on financially relevant interfaces (INT-01 to INT-05) are monitored daily and resolved; inbound and outbound files are reconciled by count and value; the payment file is protected from change after creation
SYS-03 → INT-01…05 → BP-P2P-03 / BP-O2C-02 → R-P2P-003, R-O2C-001 → C-ITGC-CO-002 → C-ITGC-CO-002-TOE

blocks.text: 30.1 What the control must achieve

W02 identified the interfaces that carry financial data. This control makes sure every record arrives once, complete and unchanged, and that errors are corrected. The payment file (INT-05) needs particular care: after SAP creates it, it sits in a directory until transmitted, and anyone who can edit it can redirect payments.
30.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: WE02 / WE05 (status 51 error, 53 posted); BD87 reprocess
Inbound IDoc errors, e.g. INT-03 EDI orders
F110 log, DMEE format tree, file directory (AL11), OS directory permissions
Count and value agreement source ↔ target

blocks.text: 30.3 Population and IPE
Daily monitoring over the period: 25 days sampled (SMP-013). Reconciliations for INT-05 per payment run: 38 runs, sample 25. All IDoc errors in status 51 older than five days at period end (EV-028).
30.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Walk through one day's monitoring for each interface.
For INT-05, trace one payment run from F110 to bank confirmation; inspect who has write access to the payment file directory at OS and AL11 level.
30.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: Daily monitoring evidenced for each in-scope interface
Errors resolved or escalated within the agreed time
Payment file total agrees to F110 total and to bank confirmation
Only the transmission service account can write to the payment directory

blocks.text: 30.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — Test A and B for 25 sampled days.
Step 2 — Test C for 25 payment runs.
Step 3 — Test D once, with the infrastructure team.
Step 4 — Review aged IDoc errors at period end for unposted financial transactions.
30.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing

rows: All totals agreed to bank confirmation
Four AP users have write access to the directory
18 ORDERS05 IDocs in status 51 for 30+ days (INT-03), value not yet quantified

blocks.text: Result: Exception noted. Directory write access (DEF-014, high, linked to R-P2P-003) and aged EDI errors that may mean revenue is unbilled (DEF-015, referred to O2C team to quantify).
30.8 Evaluating exceptions
File-level access is outside SAP authorisations; check it with infrastructure, or the payment risk is not covered.
Aged interface errors are a completeness issue for the financial statements, not only an IT matter.
If no reconciliation exists, the control relies entirely on monitoring; assess whether that is enough.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — THE INTERFACE INVENTORY PAYS OFF Without W02, the payment directory would never have been examined. The inventory built in Session 3 is what turned an infrastructure detail into a tested control.

blocks.text: Session 31 — WP-CO-03 Backup and Recovery

rows: C-ITGC-CO-003 — ECP database and logs are backed up daily, failures are resolved, and a restore is tested at least annually
ITGC-CO · Automated with manual monitoring · Daily / Annual
SYS-03 / SYS-06 → BP-TECH-03 → R-TECH-006 → C-ITGC-CO-003 → C-ITGC-CO-003-TOE

blocks.text: 31.1 What the control must achieve

If financial data is lost or corrupted it must be recoverable to a known point. Many external auditors treat backup as lower risk for SOX than access and change, but it remains in scope as an ITGC. Under a hosted or RISE model, the provider usually performs this control, and the tester relies on its SOC 1 report.
31.2 SAP navigation and data sources

rows: Evidence data can actually be restored
Provider SOC 1 Type II and bridge letter
Provider-operated controls; complementary user entity controls (CUECs)

blocks.text: 31.3 Population and IPE
Daily backups: 25 days sampled (SMP-014). Restore test: the most recent test in or near the period. Where hosted, the SOC 1 replaces direct testing of the provider's controls.
31.4 Test of design (walkthrough)
Confirm backup schedule, retention and failure alerting.
If hosted (W01 Hosting model), obtain the SOC 1, confirm period coverage, read exceptions, and map CUECs to ABC controls.
31.5 Test attributes (TOE)

rows: Backup completed successfully on sampled day, or failure resolved
Restore test performed within 12 months and successful
If SOC 1 relied on: period covered, exceptions assessed, CUECs in place

blocks.text: 31.6 Step-by-step procedure
Step 1 — Test A for 25 days.
Step 2 — Inspect B.
Step 3 — If applicable, complete the SOC 1 review in C and record any CUECs in W05 as ABC controls.
31.7 Worked result — ABC Manufacturing
Result: Effective.
31.8 Evaluating exceptions
A SOC 1 that does not cover the full period needs a bridge letter.
CUECs listed in the SOC 1 (for example, the client reviewing provider access) are the client's controls and must be tested by the client team.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — HOSTING CHANGES WHO OPERATES, NOT WHO IS ACCOUNTABLE When the provider runs a control, ABC still owns the risk. The SOC 1 review and CUEC mapping is how that accountability is demonstrated.

blocks.text: Session 32 — WP-ITAC-01 Configuration Controls

rows: C-ITAC-004 — Invoices outside OMR6 tolerances are automatically blocked for payment; only authorised AP supervisors can release blocks (MRBR). C-ITAC-005 — Posting periods in OB52 are restricted and only authorised users can change them
SYS-03 → BP-P2P-02 / BP-R2R-02 → R-P2P-002, R-R2R-001 → C-ITAC-004, C-ITAC-005 → TOD/TOE

blocks.text: 32.1 What the control must achieve

32.8 Evaluating exceptions
QAS reperformance only counts if QAS configuration is shown to equal PRD.

blocks.text: Session 33 — The ITGC Reliance Assessment
33.1 Purpose

This session brings the ITGC results together and decides, for every ITAC, IPE and ITDM control, whether reliance is supported. It is recorded in the W05 ITGC_Dependency tab and summarised in W14 ITGC_Reliance. It is the point where the golden thread from Part 1, Section 1.5 is closed.
33.2 ITGC results summary
33.3 Decision logic
For each dependent control ask three questions:
Could the control's configuration or logic have changed without authorisation? (Program Change ITGCs, system settings, privileged access.)
Could the control have been overridden? (Access to release, unblock, open or change.)
If yes to either, do additional procedures show it did not happen? (Table change logs for the full period, usage analysis of the risky users, audit log.)

If additional procedures give sufficient evidence, reliance is supported with the procedures documented. If not, reliance is not supported and the team must test the business outcome directly (substantive testing of transactions) or rely on other controls.

Documenting that reasoning is one of the most valuable things a controls consultant does, and it is only possible when the foundation workbooks link every control to its dependencies.

Session 35 — Evaluating Deficiencies
35.1 From exception to deficiency

A test exception is a fact: a sample item did not meet an attribute. A deficiency is a judgement: the control, as designed or as it operated, does not allow management to prevent or detect misstatements on a timely basis. Between the two sits evaluation, recorded in W13. Every exception follows the same path.

rows: Is the exception real? (False positive, wrong population, evidence later provided?)
Is it a design or operating failure?
Design: control would not work even if performed. Operating: control exists but was not performed as designed
Does the number of deviations exceed the tolerable rate for the sample?
Commonly 0 deviations tolerated for samples up to 25; 1 may be tolerated for larger samples with extended testing
What could go wrong, how much, how likely, which dependent controls are affected?
Do other tested, effective controls reduce the exposure?
Do several deficiencies share a cause, process or account?
Deficiency, significant deficiency or material weakness

blocks.text: 35.2 The four-part deficiency statement

rows: CONDITION — CRITERIA — CAUSE — EFFECT Condition:  what was found (facts, numbers, dates). Criteria:  what should have happened (the control description in W05, the policy). Cause:  why it happened (from inquiry with the control owner). Effect:  what could go wrong as a result, linked to the RISK-ID and assertion.

blocks.text: 35.3 Severity factors

rows: Accounts affected are below materiality; low transaction value
Isolated, explained, detected by another control
Misappropriation possible (vendor creation, payment, bank details)
No ITAC/IPE relies on it, or reliance restored by additional procedures
Reliance on ITACs/IPE cannot be restored
Tested, effective, precise enough to detect a material misstatement

blocks.text: 35.4 Evaluating ITGC deficiencies

An ITGC deficiency rarely causes a misstatement directly. Its severity is driven by what it does to the controls and reports that depend on it. The evaluation therefore always reads the W05 ITGC_Dependency tab and the Session 33 reliance decision:
If reliance on all dependent controls was restored by additional procedures, the ITGC deficiency is normally a deficiency or, if pervasive, a significant deficiency.

If reliance could not be restored and no other controls cover the risk, the ITGC deficiency takes on the severity of the business-process exposure it leaves open, and can contribute to a material weakness.
35.5 Materiality for the running case
For ABC Manufacturing, the external auditor has set overall materiality at USD 2.5 million and a clearly trivial threshold of USD 125,000. These figures are used in Session 36 to judge magnitude.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — JUDGE THE GROUP, NOT JUST THE ITEM Two or three modest deficiencies that share a root cause can together be significant. The workbook links (same user, same date, same process) are what make aggregation possible. Evaluate each DEF, then evaluate the groups.

blocks.text: Session 37 — Remediation and Retesting
37.1 Remediation plan

Each deficiency, or each aggregated group, has one remediation plan in W13, owned by the control owner and agreed with management. A good plan fixes the cause, not just the instance: removing FI_SUPPORT1's SAP_ALL fixes the instance; preventing Basis from assigning roles and opening production without approval fixes the cause.

rows: Remove SAP_ALL from all dialog users; move emergency Basis work to Firefighter; require ticket and approval for SE06/SCC4 openings with automatic alert; lock TRAINING01
Remove SOD-001/003 conflicts; reschedule F110 under a technical user; restrict payment directory to the transmission account; correct ZMM_POGR_EXCEPT logic and transport through change management
Daily HR leavers feed to GRC with auto-lock; FF reason codes made specific with mandatory controller query of master-data changes; align instance profile parameter
Ticket all critical job failures; aged IDoc alert after 3 days; enforce QAS sign-off attachment in ITSM

blocks.text: 37.2 Minimum operating period before retest
A remediated control must operate long enough to produce a meaningful sample. Typical minimums are shown below; the external auditor's methodology prevails.

rows: Until enough occurrences exist (often 30 days or more)
Once implemented, with change controls effective

blocks.text: 37.3 Retest workflow
Create a new TEST-ID in W10 (for example C-ITGC-AC-005-RT1), linked to the DEF-ID.
Request the post-remediation population in W08 and complete the IPE check in W09.
Sample (W12) from the post-remediation period only.
Complete the workpaper (W11). If effective, set DEF status to Closed with the retest reference; if not, keep it open and update severity.
Update W14 so the coverage matrix shows both the original result and the remediated position at period end.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — A FIX IS NOT A CLOSE A deficiency closes only when the retest shows the remediated control operating. Until then, W14 must show it as open, however confident management is in the fix.

blocks.text: 38.3 Writing a finding

rows: EXAMPLE FINDING — GROUP A (SIGNIFICANT DEFICIENCY) Condition:  On 14 March, a Basis administrator opened the production system for changes without an approved ticket and directly assigned roles to six users, including SAP_ALL to the dialog user FI_SUPPORT1, which remained in place until September. The June privileged-access review was not performed. Criteria:  Production is to remain closed except for approved, time-limited openings (C-ITGC-PC-002); all access is to be requested and approved through GRC (C-ITGC-AC-001); privileged access is restricted to approved users and reviewed monthly (C-ITGC-AC-005). Cause:  An urgent month-end fix was performed outside the change and access processes, and no retrospective approval or review took place. Effect:  The Basis team could bypass change and access controls, creating a risk of unauthorised changes to financial data and configuration (R-TECH-003, R-TECH-005). Table change logs and user activity analysis for the full period found no unauthorised changes to financial configuration and no misuse of the access. Management response:  Agreed. Actions and dates per remediation plan Group A.

blocks.text: A finding uses plain language, states facts with numbers and dates, cites the control (not the tester's opinion) as criteria, and says what was done to assess the impact. It never names individuals in a report circulated beyond the control owners; user IDs are given in the workpaper, not the report.

blocks.text: 40.2 Ten principles to take away
The thread is the product: every conclusion traces back to a server, and every server traces forward to a conclusion.
Modules are not processes; processes are not controls; control areas are not controls.
Risks are written before controls, and controls before evidence requests.
Never invent scope; mark it TBC and follow it up.
Populations come from the system of record: production for changes, HR for leavers, the full user master for access.
Test the population before the sample.
Every report relied on is IPE and is tested for completeness and accuracy.
ITGCs are tested first because ITACs and IPE rely on them.
A failed ITGC removes the presumption of reliance; evidence can restore it.
Evaluate groups, not just items, and close a deficiency only on a successful retest.

About This Course
Purpose

The five-part manual "Building the SAP Controls Project Foundation" teaches the method of a controls project. It assumes you can already work comfortably in the 14 Excel workbooks that carry that method. This course gets you there. It teaches how the workbooks are built, how to enter and read data in them, how they check themselves, and how they connect to each other. It is a prerequisite: finish it before you start Session 1 of the manual.
Who it is for

New consultants, analysts and testers joining a controls team, and new controls leads who want to understand the tools their team uses. You need only basic Excel: opening files, moving between tabs, typing in cells, and saving.

blocks.text: 1.1 What a register is

Every workbook in the set is built around one or more registers. A register is a table in which each row is one thing (a risk, a control, a test, a deficiency) and each column is one fact about it (its owner, its category, its status). The first column is almost always the key: a unique code that identifies the row, such as R-P2P-006 for a risk or DEF-007 for a deficiency. Other workbooks refer to the row by that key, never by its description.

sections.title: Session 2 — Entering Data and Pasting Values

blocks.text: Session 2 — Entering Data and Pasting Values

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Use dropdowns and understand the two kinds of validation. Enter keys, dates and numbers so the checks accept them. Paste values only into Ref_ tabs, from the correct source cells.

blocks.text: 2.1 Dropdowns

Many input cells carry a dropdown. Click the cell and a small arrow appears. The list comes from the hidden Lists tab or from another tab in the workbook. Dropdowns exist so that everyone spells a value the same way; the checks and counts depend on exact matches.
There are two kinds, and the difference matters:

rows: What happens if you type something not on the list
Excel refuses it and shows "Pick a value from the list"
Excel warns, but lets you continue
Keys that must exist in another workbook

blocks.text: A warning is not permission. The row check beside the record tells you if the key is not found.
2.2 Keys, text, dates and numbers

Keys: type them exactly as they appear in the source workbook, with the same capital letters, hyphens and numbers. R-P2P-006 and r-p2p-006 may look the same to you but a stray space or a missing hyphen breaks a lookup. Never renumber a key; if a row leaves scope, mark it out of scope and leave the key.
Dates: type a real date (for example 31-May-2026 or 2026-05-31) so Excel right-aligns it. A date typed as text, left-aligned, will not compare correctly in formulas such as days overdue.
Numbers: type a number without units or words. 25 is a number; "25 items" is text and a sample-size check will not read it.
Y and N: use the dropdown values exactly: Y, N (and TBC where offered).
2.3 Paste values only
Workbooks do not link to each other. Instead, the keys you need from an upstream workbook are pasted into a Ref_ tab in the downstream workbook. You must paste values only:
Copy the cells from the source workbook.
Click the first cell of the target (A2 on a Ref_ tab; the headers are in row 1).
Use Paste Special and choose Values (Ctrl+Alt+V, then V, then Enter).

Why values? A normal paste would carry formulas that point to the source file and break the moment the file moves, or it would bring formatting and validation that overwrite the target. A value is just the key, which is all the Ref_ tab needs.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — COPY ONLY THE ROWS THAT HAVE KEYS In W03, the BP_Index tab lists keys by formula. The 14 business keys sit in rows 5 to 18 and the four technical keys sit in rows 155 to 158, with blank formula cells between them. If you copy the whole column you also paste empty text into the Ref_ tab. Copy the two blocks separately and paste them one under the other.

blocks.text: 2.4 Never overwrite a grey cell
If you type over a formula, the check or lookup in that cell stops working for that row. Repair it by copying the formula from the row above and pasting it into the damaged cell.

sections.title: Session 3 — The Formulas You Will Meet

blocks.text: Session 3 — The Formulas You Will Meet

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Find and read a formula in a grey cell. Explain five functions: IF, COUNTIF, SUMPRODUCT, INDEX with MATCH, and IFERROR. Read a row check from its first condition to its last.

blocks.text: 3.1 How to see a formula

Click a grey cell and read the formula bar above the sheet. Press F2 to edit in the cell and Esc to leave without changing anything. You do not need to write these formulas, only to read them well enough to explain what the cell is telling you.
3.2 Five functions in plain language
IF: choose between answers
IF(test, answer if true, answer if false). In W04 the Rating band column turns the number in Inherent rating into a word:
=IF(J5="","",IF(J5>=6,"High",IF(J5>=3,"Medium","Low")))

Read it: if the rating is empty, show nothing; otherwise if it is 6 or more show High; otherwise if it is 3 or more show Medium; otherwise show Low. For R-TECH-008 the rating is 3, so the band is Medium.
The rating itself is a multiplication wrapped in an IF that waits until both inputs exist:
COUNTIF: count matching rows
COUNTIF(range, value) counts how many cells in a range equal a value. In W05 the Risks mapped column counts how many risk links point to this control:
=IF(A5="","",COUNTIF(Risk_Control_Map!$C$5:$C$204,A5))
Read it: look in column C of the Risk_Control_Map tab, rows 5 to 204, and count the cells equal to this control's key. A result of 0 means the control addresses no risk, which the row check flags.
INDEX with MATCH: look something up
MATCH finds which row holds a key; INDEX returns the value from another column of that row. W07 pulls the control title from its Ref_CTRL tab:
=IFERROR(INDEX(Ref_CTRL!$B$2:$B$201,MATCH(A5,Ref_CTRL!$A$2:$A$201,0)),"")

Read it: find the row in Ref_CTRL column A where the key equals A5; return column B of that same row; and if nothing is found, show nothing (that is what IFERROR does). If a lookup cell is blank, check that the key exists in the Ref_ tab and was pasted as a value.
SUMPRODUCT: count with several conditions
The duplicate check on every Checks tab uses SUMPRODUCT to count rows whose key appears more than once:
=SUMPRODUCT((Risk_Register!A5:A204<>"")*(COUNTIF(Risk_Register!A5:A204,Risk_Register!A5:A204)>1))
Read it: for each row, ask whether the key is not empty and whether it appears more than once; multiply the two answers (1 means yes, 0 means no) and add them up. The result should be 0.
TODAY: a date that moves
Some cells, such as Days overdue in W08, use TODAY(). They change every day, so the numbers you see tomorrow may differ from today.
3.3 Reading a row check
A Row check cell is a chain of IF tests. Excel works through them in order and shows the message of the first test that fails. Here is the order for the W01 System_Inventory row check:

rows: SID, client and environment are all filled
If In scope is N, a rationale is given
If Validated, an evidence reference is given
If not Validated, an open question is given
A financial PRD system is in scope
PRD financial system should be in scope

blocks.text: Because the first failing test wins, fix the messages in the order they appear. Fixing the first often changes the message to the next.

blocks.text: 4.3 The Instructions tab

Every workbook opens on its Instructions tab. It has the same sections each time: Purpose, How to use this workbook, Colour legend, Completion gate, Manual reference, and a Column dictionary. The dictionary lists every field of every register with its definition and its rule, and says whether the column is an input or a formula. Where a column takes a dropdown the rule says so, and often names the values; the full list of values is in the dropdown itself and on the hidden Lists tab. When you are unsure what a column wants, look it up there before you ask.
4.4 Hidden tabs

The Lists tab is hidden so that it does not distract. To see it, right-click any tab, choose Unhide and pick Lists. Open it only to add or change a dropdown value. Keep each list in one unbroken column, with no gaps, because the dropdown reads a fixed range. Re-hide the tab when you finish.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — KNOW WHICH TABS YOU TYPE IN In every workbook, you type in the register tabs, you paste values into the Ref_ tabs, and you read everything else. If you are unsure, look for the yellow cells: where there are none, there is nothing to type.

blocks.text: Session 5 — Reading the Checks

rows: LEARNING OUTCOMES Tell a row check from the Checks tab and say what each is for. Read the five statuses and act on each. Explain why a fresh template can show REVIEW and a finished file shows ALL CHECKS PASS.

blocks.text: 5.1 Two levels of checking

Each workbook checks itself at two levels. The Row check (or Check) column beside each record tests that one record is complete and its keys exist. The Checks tab tests the whole workbook against its completion gate, for example that no key is duplicated, that every process has a risk, and that nothing is sampled from a population that failed its IPE check. Fix row checks first; most Checks tab lines depend on them.
5.2 The five statuses

rows: The count is zero where zero is required, or above zero where a minimum is required
A gate condition is not yet met

Index the evidence in W09 and enter the ID
HOLD: IPE not Pass - do not sample

Complete the IPE log; then sample

Change it or record a reason

sections.title: 5.4 A fresh template can show REVIEW; a finished file does not

blocks.text: 5.4 A fresh template can show REVIEW; a finished file does not

Open the blank W04 template and its Checks tab shows REVIEW on two lines: "In-scope BP-IDs with no risk" (the template lists the 12 sample processes but holds only one risk) and "Technical-area risks recorded" (none yet). That is correct: gate conditions are not met until real records are entered. Not every blank template shows REVIEW, because some hold example rows that already satisfy their checks; the point is that REVIEW means a gate condition is genuinely unmet. In the completed Corvane files every Checks tab reads ALL CHECKS PASS.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — CHECKS MEASURE COMPLETENESS, NOT CORRECTNESS A row can read OK and still be wrong. The checks prove that a key exists, a field is filled and a rule is met. They cannot prove that the owner is the right owner or that a control description is true. A passing workbook is ready for review, not finished with thinking.

blocks.text: 12.1 Why trace

A controls project is only as good as its traceability. A reviewer will pick any deficiency and ask where it came from, or pick any system and ask what was done about it. If you can answer either question in a few steps, the foundation is sound. The trace uses only keys: you move from one to the next by reading them off a row.

The assessment tests the skills in this course. It has three sections and is worth 100 marks. The pass mark is 80. Use your own copy of the Corvane folder and give yourself 90 minutes.

4. Aggregate related deficiencies in Groups (same user, date, process or cause) and evaluate the group.
5. Record management response, owner and due date; add the retest TEST-ID. A deficiency closes only after a successful retest.

1. Purpose and Scope

This guide explains how to deploy the fourteen Excel workbooks that define the foundation of an SAP controls project: from the landscape (W01) to the conclusion (W14). It covers the package contents, how to set up an engagement folder, how the workbooks connect to each other, the order in which they are populated, how to read their built-in checks, who does what, and how to handle evidence. It is written for engagement managers, senior consultants and course instructors. The manual explains why each workbook exists and how to fill it; this guide explains how to run the set as a whole.

rows: THE ONE IDEA TO HOLD ON TO Every workbook carries a unique key, and every downstream workbook carries the keys of the rows it depends on. The workbooks do not link to each other through Excel links. Instead, the keys you need from upstream are pasted as values into the small Ref_ tabs of the downstream workbook. That keeps each file independent and portable, and it puts one disciplined step between every stage: the paste.

blocks.text: 2.2 Workbooks
2.3 What every workbook contains
Instructions tab: purpose, how to use, colour legend, completion gate, and a column dictionary (definition and allowed values for every field).
Register tabs: yellow input cells with blue text, grey formula cells, dropdowns, frozen header, filter, and a worked ABC Manufacturing example in the first row(s).
Ref_ tabs: where you paste keys from upstream workbooks.
Checks tab: the workbook's completion gate as formulas (PASS, REVIEW, INFO, plus HOLD and SCOPING where relevant).
Hidden Lists tab: the dropdown values. Visible, editable lists exist where users are expected to maintain them (Control_Areas in W05, Sample_Guide in W10, Templates in W11).
3. Setting Up an Engagement
3.1 Folder structure
Create one folder per engagement, with the following subfolders. Keep the workbooks together so that every team member opens the same version.

rows: Engagement letter, scope statement, contact list, this guide
W01–W14, one file each, plus an Archive subfolder for superseded versions

blocks.text: 3.2 Naming and versioning
Keep the file names exactly as supplied so that references in the manual and in instructions remain valid.
Version by saving a dated copy into the Archive subfolder at each gate (for example W05_G4_2026-10-14.xlsx). The live file keeps the standard name.
Evidence files follow the W09 convention: EV-ID_SYS_description_date.ext (for example EV-019_ECP_STMS_import_history_2026-10-01.csv).
3.3 Excel settings
Use a current desktop version of Excel. Keep automatic calculation on. The checks rely on formulas that recalculate as you type.
Do not sort the register tabs by dragging a selection. Use the filter buttons; sorting only part of a table breaks the row formulas.
Do not delete the grey formula columns. If a formula column is damaged, copy the formula down from the row above.
Optional: protect the sheets with the grey columns locked and the yellow cells unlocked, so formula cells cannot be overwritten. This is not applied in the templates so that they stay easy to adapt.
4. How the Workbooks Connect
4.1 The paste rule

Each downstream workbook has one or more Ref_ tabs with a header describing exactly what to paste. The rule is simple: copy the named columns from the upstream workbook and paste them into the Ref_ tab as values only (Paste Special > Values), starting at cell A2. Do not paste formulas, and do not paste the header row. The yellow cells hold ABC Manufacturing sample values that you overwrite.

blocks.text: 4.3 Keeping references in sync

Re-paste at every gate. Upstream data changes (a new control, a changed owner). Before reading a downstream Checks tab, re-paste the Ref_ tab. A stale Ref_ tab is the most common cause of confusing results.
Keys never change. If a row leaves scope, set In scope = N and keep the key. Renumbering breaks every link downstream.
Create new items at source. A new risk or control is added to W04 or W05 first and then re-pasted downstream. It is never created only in a workpaper.
Capacity. Registers hold 200 rows (W12 Items holds 1,000); Ref_ tabs hold 200 keys. See section 9 for extending them.
5. Reading the Built-In Checks
5.1 Row checks

Most registers have a Row check or Check column (grey). It tests completeness, not correctness: for example, "Evidence ref needed" or "Use the risk statement formula". A row passes when it reads OK (or begins with OK, such as "OK (test pending)"). Filter the column to anything that is not OK and work through the list.
5.2 The Checks tab

They clear as the real records are entered. If a check still shows REVIEW after entry, it is telling you something true about the engagement.

blocks.text: 6. Rollout Sequence and Gates
Follow the sequence below. Each stage has a gate: do not start the next stage until the gate is passed. The gates are the same as in Session 16 of the manual.

rows: W01 and W02 Checks: all financially relevant systems and interfaces listed; validated or flagged; PRD transport route recorded
W03 Checks: every significant FSLI mapped; technical areas BP-TECH-01 to 03 present; unspecified processes Outstanding, not guessed
W04 Checks: no BP-ID without a risk; SOX risks flagged; owners agreed
W05 Coverage_Check: no SOX risk without a key control; ITGC dependencies recorded. W06 Checks: every SoD risk has a rule; ruleset approved
W07 Checks: owners confirmed or escalated. Issue W14 in scoping form: "No conclusion at scoping stage"
W09 Checks: populations received; every IPE result Pass
W10 Checks: TOD and TOE for every key control; ITGC tests scheduled first
W12 and W11 Checks: samples logged; workpapers reviewed; exceptions carry a DEF-ID or rationale
W13 Checks and W14 Checks with Stage = Testing: all coverage checks pass; conclusion signed

blocks.text: 6.1 Scoping deliverable versus testing deliverable

Stages 1 to 5, plus the wave 1 and 2 evidence requests, make up the scope of work. At gate G5, W14 is issued with Stage = Scoping. Stages 6 to 9 are the testing phase that the scope of work plans and controls. Keep the G5 versions of W01–W08 and W14 in the Archive folder as the formal scope record.
6.2 Iteration

The sequence is not strictly one-way. A walkthrough in stage 3 may reveal an interface missing from W02, or a test may show a control works differently from its RCM description. Update the source workbook, keep the keys, re-paste downstream, and let the checks show the effect. Never patch a downstream workbook to cover an upstream gap.
7. Roles and Responsibilities

rows: Scope, gates, severity approval, final conclusion; owns W14
Risk and control design, SoD ruleset, reliance assessment, deficiency evaluation
Evidence requests, indexing, IPE checks, sampling, workpapers
Independent review of workpapers and results; must differ from the tester
Single point of contact; tracks requests and dependencies with the client
System facts, extracts, transport routes, interface mechanics
Confirm processes, risks, controls, owners, evidence

blocks.text: In a training lab, the instructor plays the client coordinator and the engagement manager; trainees take the tester and senior consultant roles, working in pairs so that each has a reviewer.
8. Evidence Handling and Confidentiality
Raw originals are read-only. Store each file as received in 02_Evidence_Raw and record Original preserved = Y in W09. Work only on copies.

Extracts contain personal and sensitive data (user lists, payroll, vendor bank details). Store them only in the engagement folder, restrict folder access to the engagement team, and do not send them by unprotected email.
Do not include personal data in reports. User IDs belong in workpapers; reports refer to roles and counts.

Record how every extract was produced. W09 asks who ran it, when and how. Where possible, watch the extract being run, or capture the selection parameters in a screenshot with the system and date visible.
Retain per policy. Agree the retention and secure deletion of evidence with the client at the start of the engagement.
Client and ISP names. Use the real client names in engagement documents. Fictitious names are used only in the training manual's ABC Manufacturing case.
9. Customising the Templates
9.1 Extending capacity

More rows in a register: copy the last data row (including formulas, formatting and data validation) and paste it below. Then extend the ranges used by the Checks tab by editing the row limit in its formulas (the registers use rows 5 to 204).

More keys in a Ref_ tab: the Ref_ tabs and their lookups cover rows 2 to 201. For more than 200 keys, split the engagement into two sets of workbooks (for example, by system) rather than extending ranges everywhere.
9.2 Editing lists and guides
Control_Areas (W05) and Templates (W11) are visible lists: add or rename entries.
Sample_Guide (W10): edit the low and high sample sizes to match the engagement firm or the external auditor's methodology. The manual's values are typical practice, not a standard.
Dropdown lists elsewhere are on the hidden Lists tab. Unhide it, edit the values, and keep the list items in a single contiguous column.
9.3 Adding columns

Add new columns to the right of the last column (after the Row check column), never in the middle. Inserting a column shifts the letters that the row checks and the Checks tab depend on. If you must insert a column, update every formula that refers to the columns to its right.

sections.title: 9.4 Adding a second landscape or entity

blocks.text: 9.4 Adding a second landscape or entity

Use a separate set of fourteen workbooks for a separate legal entity or a separate SAP landscape. Combine results in W14 by pasting both sets into its Ref_ tabs with distinct key prefixes (for example, SYS-A-01 and SYS-B-01).

sections.title: Session 1 — The Foundation and the Golden Thread

blocks.text: Session 1 — The Foundation and the Golden Thread
1.1 What this manual teaches

A controls project does not begin with testing. It begins with a set of linked Excel workbooks that define, without ambiguity, what is being tested, why, against which risk, using which evidence, and by whom. If that foundation is weak, every test that follows is weak: samples are pulled from the wrong system, controls are tested that address no risk, and evidence cannot be traced back to scope when a reviewer or external auditor asks.

This manual walks a trainee through the full foundation, one workbook at a time. For each workbook it explains what the workbook is for, how it is structured, every data field and its allowed values, where the data comes from, how it is populated, and how it links to the workbooks before and after it. By the end of the series, a trainee should be able to start from a single SAP server and follow the thread to every test step performed for SOX, ITGC and ITAC purposes, and back again.
1.2 The fourteen workbooks

The Lab 1 scoping draft used six workbooks. This manual expands that set to fourteen so the thread continues past scoping into risk, control, test and conclusion. The workbooks are grouped into five phases.

rows: What SAP systems, clients and servers exist, and which are in scope?
How does financially relevant data move into, out of and between systems?
Which business processes run in which modules, on which systems?
What could go wrong in each process or technical area, and who owns that risk?
Which specific control addresses each risk, and how is it classified?
Which combinations of access are conflicting or sensitive?
Who operates each control and who can supply the evidence?
What evidence is requested, from whom, for which period and which control?
What was received, is it complete and accurate, and where is it filed?
How, when and by whom will each control be tested (design and operating effectiveness)?
What exactly was done, on which items, with what result?
Which items were selected from which population, and how?
What failed, how severe is it, and how is it being fixed?
Is every risk covered, every key control tested, every gap visible?

blocks.text: Part 1 (this document) covers Session 1 and workbooks W01–W05. Part 2 covers W06–W14 and the population sequence. Parts 3A and 3B cover testing by control area. Part 4 covers deficiency evaluation and the end-to-end trace exercise.
1.3 The golden thread
Every workbook carries a unique primary key, and every downstream workbook carries the keys of the rows it depends on. This is the golden thread. It is what makes a controls project auditable.
SYS → INT → BP → RISK → CTRL → OWNER → PBC → EV → TEST → SMP → DEF → CONCLUSION

Read it left to right to plan: start from what exists and work toward what must be tested. Read it right to left to defend: start from any test conclusion and prove which evidence, control, risk, process and system it rests on.
Identifier conventions

rows: Three-way match configuration   Termination of access
Terminated users list for the period

CORE INSIGHT — THE THREAD IS THE PRODUCT A reviewer does not judge a controls project by the number of tests performed. They judge it by whether any single conclusion can be traced, in both directions, without gaps. A test that cannot be traced to a risk is wasted effort. A risk that cannot be traced to a test is an unreported exposure.

blocks.text: 1.4 How the records relate
The relationships between workbooks are not all one-to-one. Trainees must understand the cardinality, because it decides how rows are built.
One system supports many processes; one process can run on several systems. W03 therefore lists the supporting SYS-IDs on each process row.
One process has many risks. Each risk row in W04 carries exactly one BP-ID (or a technical-area BP-ID such as BP-TECH-01).

Risks and controls are many-to-many. One control (for example, the quarterly user access review) can mitigate several risks, and one risk can need more than one control. W05 handles this with a separate Risk-to-Control mapping tab.
Every control is tested twice in principle: once for design (TOD, also called walkthrough) and once for operating effectiveness (TOE). W10 creates both test rows for each in-scope key control.
One control can draw on several PBC requests, and one PBC request (for example, the full user master extract) can serve several controls.

sections.title: 1.5 Control categories and how SOX scope applies

blocks.text: 1.5 Control categories and how SOX scope applies

A common misunderstanding is that each control is tested "for ITGC, for ITAC and for SOX". That is not how scoping works. Each control is classified into one category. SOX relevance is a separate flag on the control that decides whether formal design and operating-effectiveness testing is required for the financial statement audit.

rows: Who can get into the system and what they can do
User provisioning, termination, periodic user access review, privileged and generic IDs, Firefighter/emergency access, SoD, password and logon parameters
Transport approval and migration (STMS), segregation of developer and migrator, client and system change settings (SCC4, SE06), direct changes in production, debug-and-replace
Batch job scheduling and monitoring (SM37), interface monitoring, backup and restore, incident management
Data migration reconciliation, go-live approval, testing sign-off (applies only when a project is in the audit period)
Three-way match and tolerance limits, duplicate invoice check, posting period control (OB52), credit limit check, field status groups, automatic account determination
IPE — Information Produced by the Entity

Vendor master change report, aged debt report, user listings used in access reviews
Business-process controls performed by people, sometimes using system output
Review of GR/IR clearing, bank reconciliation review, journal entry approval

blocks.text: The reliance link

ITGCs are not tested for their own sake. They are tested because automated controls and system reports can only be trusted if the environment that runs them is controlled. If a developer can change the three-way match configuration in production without approval, a clean test of the three-way match proves nothing about the rest of the year. This is why every ITAC, IPE and ITDM row in the RCM records its dependent ITGCs, and why ITGC results are evaluated before reliance is placed on automated controls.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — ITGCs PROTECT ITACs An ITAC that passes testing is reliable only for the period during which the related ITGCs (especially Program Change and APD over configuration) were also effective. A failed ITGC does not automatically fail the ITAC, but it removes the basis for a single "test of one" and forces additional work. Session 6 shows how this is recorded.

sections.title: 1.6 Rules that apply to every workbook

blocks.text: 1.6 Rules that apply to every workbook
Never invent. If the source does not specify a value, enter TBC and record the open question. A guessed value contaminates every downstream link.
Separate known from unconfirmed. Every workbook has a status or validation column for this purpose.
No effectiveness conclusion during scoping. A missing owner, a missing report or an unvalidated system is a dependency, not a control failure.
Keys are never reused or renumbered. If a row is removed from scope, set In Scope = N and keep the key.
Preserve raw evidence. Indexed copies are worked on; originals are never overwritten.
One fact, one home. A value such as a system owner lives in one workbook; others refer to it by key rather than retyping it.
Session 2 — W01 Landscape & System Inventory
2.1 Purpose

W01 records every SAP system, client and supporting component that holds financial data or processes business transactions, and states for each one whether it is in scope and whether its existence and configuration have actually been validated. It is the root of the golden thread: every other workbook ultimately points back to a SYS-ID.

The workbook exists to stop scoping from resting on a landscape diagram alone. Diagrams are often out of date, omit sandbox or legacy clients, and do not show where production data has been copied. W01 reconciles what the client says exists with what the consultant can confirm.

blocks.text: 2.5 How W01 is populated

Step 1 — Collect the client view. Request the landscape diagram, system inventory, hosting contract summary and the list of SAP products licensed. Enter every listed component with Validation status = Documented only.

Step 2 — Validate directly where access allows. For each accessible system run System > Status (SID, client, release), SCC4 (clients and their change settings), SM51 (application servers) and, through Basis, DB02 (database). Capture screenshots with the date and system visible. Update the row to Validated and enter the evidence reference.
Step 3 — Capture transport routes. Ask Basis for the STMS transport route display. Record the route in the Transport_Routes tab. This is the starting point for every Program Change test later.

Step 4 — Decide scope. Mark every financially relevant production system In scope = Y. Mark DEV and QAS in scope where they are needed as evidence sources (transport origin, approvals). Exclude sandboxes and training clients with a written rationale.
Step 5 — Record what is still open. Any row that is Documented only or To confirm generates an Open_Items entry with an owner and a target date.
2.6 Common errors
Listing systems from the diagram only and marking them validated without evidence.
Recording the SID but not the client; ECP/300 and ECP/400 can hold entirely different data and access populations.
Forgetting the database layer. HANA and OS-level privileged users bypass SAP application security and must be scoped for APD.
Omitting GRC and Fiori because they do not post transactions. GRC is where Firefighter and access request evidence lives.
Ignoring the hosting model. Under RISE or a managed service, some ITGCs are performed by the provider and are covered by a SOC 1 report rather than direct testing.
2.7 Completion gate

rows: W01 IS COMPLETE WHEN Every known component is listed with SID, client and environment. Every row has In scope = Y/N with a rationale for N. Every Validated row has an evidence reference; every other row has an open question. The PRD transport route is recorded. Downstream workbooks can now reference SYS-IDs.

sections.title: Session 3 — W02 Interface & Data Flow Inventory

blocks.text: Session 3 — W02 Interface & Data Flow Inventory
3.1 Purpose

Financial data does not only enter SAP through people typing transactions. Bank statements, payroll postings, customer orders and master data often arrive through interfaces. If an interface drops, duplicates or alters records, the financial statements are wrong even though every SAP user control worked perfectly. W02 identifies each financially relevant interface, how it works, how errors are caught and who owns it.
W02 also captures the technical plumbing that matters for access: RFC destinations with stored credentials and the system or service users behind them are themselves privileged access paths.

File could be altered after creation; high-risk

blocks.text: 3.5 How W02 is populated
Step 1 — Ask by process, not by technology. For each in-scope process ask: what data comes in from outside SAP, and what leaves? Business owners know the flows; Basis knows the mechanics.

Step 2 — Confirm the mechanism. With Basis or integration support, review partner profiles (WE20), RFC destinations (SM59), PI/PO or CPI integration lists and scheduled file jobs (SM37). Record the technology and the technical user.
Step 3 — Ask how failures are detected. For each interface, ask who looks at errors, how often and what evidence exists. Record the honest answer, including "nobody".
Step 4 — Flag financially relevant interfaces. Anything posting to the GL, creating payables or receivables, or transmitting payments is financially relevant.
Step 5 — Back-fill BP-IDs once W03 is built, so each interface points to the process it supports.
3.6 Common errors
Skipping outbound files. The payment file leaving SAP is one of the highest fraud risks in the landscape.
Treating RFC connections as "infrastructure only". Stored credentials in SM59 and over-privileged RFC users are access risks.
Recording monitoring as "yes" without identifying who, how often and what evidence.
Ignoring manual mass uploads (LSMW, LTMC, custom upload programs), which behave like interfaces without the controls.
3.7 Completion gate

rows: W02 IS COMPLETE WHEN Every financially relevant inbound and outbound flow is listed. Every interface has a technology, a monitoring answer and an owner (or TBC). RFC/service users are listed and cross-referenced. Interfaces with no monitoring or reconciliation are clearly visible for risk assessment in W04.

sections.title: Session 4 — W03 Module & Business Process Scope

blocks.text: Session 4 — W03 Module & Business Process Scope
4.1 Purpose

W03 separates the SAP module from the business process, and ties each process to the system it runs on and the financial statement areas it affects. FI/CO, MM, SD, HCM and Basis/Security are modules or functional areas. Procure-to-Pay, Order-to-Cash, Record-to-Report and Inventory are business processes. A process often crosses modules: Procure-to-Pay uses MM for purchasing and goods receipt and FI for invoice posting and payment.
The BP-ID created here is the anchor for every risk in W04. A risk without a BP-ID has no home.
4.2 Workbook structure

rows: Significant financial statement line items and accounts mapped to processes
Basis/Security technical areas treated as processes for ITGC purposes
Processes or owners still to confirm

blocks.text: 4.3 Data fields — Process_Scope tab

rows: R2R / P2P / O2C / INV / H2R / TECH
SAP modules or functional areas used
FI, CO, MM, SD, HCM, Basis/Security (multi-select)
Why it matters to the audit
e.g. XK01/BP, ME21N, MIGO, MIRO, F110
Used later for SoD and access testing
Reason for inclusion or open question

blocks.text: 4.4 Worked example — ABC Manufacturing

The Week 1 source identifies Finance, Procure-to-Pay, Inventory and Order-to-Cash as in-scope processes. HR is listed as a module but no HR business process is specified, so it is marked Outstanding rather than guessed.

rows: CORE INSIGHT — WHY TECHNICAL AREAS GET A BP-ID ITGC risks (access, change, operations) are not owned by a business process; they cut across all of them. Giving them technical-area BP-IDs (BP-TECH-nn) lets ITGC risks follow exactly the same thread as business risks, so the RCM, test plan and coverage dashboard treat them consistently.

blocks.text: 4.5 How W03 is populated
Step 1 — Start from the financial statements. Obtain the significant accounts and FSLIs from the audit plan or management's SOX scoping. Enter them in FSLI_Map.

Step 2 — Map each significant account to the process that creates its balance. Trade payables comes from P2P; revenue and receivables from O2C; inventory from INV; every account is affected by R2R journals and close.
Step 3 — Break each process into sub-processes and assign a BP-ID to each. Use the client's own process narratives where they exist.
Step 4 — Record modules, systems, interfaces and indicative transactions. Confirm transactions with process owners or with a transaction usage report (ST03N / STAD) where available.
Step 5 — Add the technical areas BP-TECH-01 to BP-TECH-03 for every in-scope landscape.
Step 6 — Mark confirmation status honestly. Source-identified means a document says so; Confirmed means an owner has agreed it.
4.6 Common errors
Listing modules as if they were processes ("FI is in scope").
Inventing a process the case does not specify, instead of marking it Outstanding.
Not linking interfaces, so the payment file or payroll journal falls outside every process.
Omitting the technical areas, which leaves ITGC risks with no anchor.
4.7 Completion gate

rows: W03 IS COMPLETE WHEN Every significant FSLI maps to at least one in-scope process. Every sub-process has a BP-ID, modules, SYS-IDs and a confirmation status. Technical areas BP-TECH-01 to 03 exist. Unspecified processes are marked Outstanding, not guessed.

blocks.text: Session 5 — W04 Risk Register
5.1 Purpose

W04 states, for each in-scope process and technical area, what could go wrong that would cause a misstatement in the financial statements or a breach of the integrity of financial data. Each risk has a named risk owner: the person accountable for the outcome if the risk materialises. The risk register is a statement of exposure, not a finding. Nothing in W04 says a control has failed.
5.2 Risk owner versus control owner

These are often confused. The risk owner is accountable for the business outcome, for example the Head of Accounts Payable owns the risk of paying a fictitious vendor. The control owner (recorded in W05 and W07) is accountable for performing a specific control, for example the AP supervisor who reviews vendor master changes. One risk owner may rely on several control owners. A risk owner without any control owner beneath them is an uncovered risk.
5.3 Writing a risk statement
Use a consistent structure so risks are comparable and testable:

rows: RISK STATEMENT FORMULA There is a risk that  [event / condition]  because  [cause or access path]  resulting in  [financial impact or assertion affected]. Example: There is a risk that a fictitious vendor is created and paid  because  one user can both maintain vendor master data and execute the payment run,  resulting in  fraudulent payments and overstated expenses (Occurrence).

blocks.text: 5.4 Data fields

rows: Process or technical area the risk belongs to
System or interface where the risk arises
ITGC-APD / ITGC-PC / ITGC-CO / ITGC-PD / ITAC / SoD / Business process / IPE / Interface
Dropdown; guides control category in W05
Occurrence, Completeness, Accuracy, Cut-off, Valuation, Existence, Rights & obligations, Presentation
At least one for SOX-relevant risks
Could lead to a material misstatement
Client RCM / framework library / walkthrough / prior-year audit issue
Draft / Agreed with owner / Dependency open

blocks.text: 5.5 Worked example — ABC Manufacturing

rows: A user can create a vendor and pay it, enabling fictitious vendor payments
An invoice is posted and paid without a matching PO and goods receipt within tolerance
The payment file is altered between creation and transmission to the bank
Postings are made to a closed accounting period

Where Part 2 sits in the golden thread

Part 1 built SYS → INT → BP → RISK → CTRL (W01–W05). Part 2 completes the thread: the access rules that make SoD and sensitive-access risks testable (W06), the people behind each control (W07), the evidence layer (W08–W09), the test layer (W10–W12) and the conclusion layer (W13–W14). Session 16 then sets out the order in which all fourteen workbooks are populated and the checkpoints between them.
